en: The Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad. Now begins the Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad.

The General Upaniṣad of the Sāmaveda I am that Great Splendor, the state of three steps (tripada) which sages attain through the awakening to Brahman alone, joined with devotion arising from dispassion. Om! May my limbs, speech, breath, sight, hearing, as well as strength and the senses, be nourished.

All is the Upanishad of Brahman, the All. May I not reject Brahman, and may Brahman not reject me. Let there be no rejection; let there be non-rejection for me. May those qualities which are in the Upanishads abide in me who is devoted to the Self; may they abide in me. Om. Peace! Peace! Peace! The Maitrāyaṇī, Kauṣītaki, Bṛhajjābāla, Tāpanī, Kālāgnirudra, Maitreyī, Subāla, Kṣurika, and Mantrikā.

Oṃ. There was indeed a king named Bṛhadratha. Having installed his eldest son in the kingdom and considering this world to be impermanent, he attained a state of physical detachment and went forth into the forest. There, having undertaken supreme austerity, he stood with arms upraised gazing at the sun. At the end of a thousand years, a sage approached him—one who was like smokeless fire, as if burning with splendor, the venerable Śākāyanya, the knower of the Self. He said to the king, "Arise, arise! Choose a boon. To him—

Having paid homage, he said: "O Blessed One, I am not a knower of the Self; you are a knower of reality. We have heard of you—do you speak to us? [Śākāyanya replied: "This was requested of me previously, but it is impossible. Do not ask this question, O descendant of Ikṣvāku; choose other boons. While touching the feet of Śākāyanya, the king uttered this verse: 1. "The wealth of a man who has a hundred horses like Saivya, or the wealth of a man who possesses a kingdom like that of the King of Kāśī—that is not worth even a sixteenth part of the sight of the True Self. || 1 ||

O Blessed One, what is the use of the enjoyment of sensual pleasures in this body which is defiled by bone, skin, sinew, marrow, flesh, semen, blood, phlegm, tears, feces, urine, wind, bile, and phlegm; which is foul-smelling, unsubstantial, and a mere collection of elements? (2) What is the use of the enjoyment of sensual pleasures in this body which is afflicted by desire, anger, greed, fear, despair, envy, separation from the beloved, union with the unpleasant, hunger, thirst, old age, death, disease, sorrow, and the like? (3)

And we see that all this is subject to decay, just as these gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like perish like blades of grass, arising only to be destroyed. Now, what of these others—those other great archers and universal monarchs (cakravartins), such as Sudyumna, Bhūridyumna, Indradyumna, Kuvalayāśva, Yauvanāśva, Śvāśvapati, Śaśabindu, Hāriścandra, Ambarīṣa, Yayāti, Naraṇyu, Ukṣasena, Utkalamarutta, Bharata, and so forth? Surely they were seen by those who watched.

Having abandoned the great prosperity of their circle of kinsmen, they depart from this world for that other world. Furthermore, what need is there to mention others? We observe the cessation of Gandharvas, Asuras, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, hosts of Bhūtas, Piśācas, Uragas, Grahas, and so forth.

Now, what is the use of these enjoyments of desire in this world characterized by such things as the drying up of other great oceans, the falling of mountains, the shaking or the stationary state of the Pole Star (Dhruva), the sinking of trees, the earth’s departure from its place, and the displacement of the gods? For those who resort to them, repeated wandering here is observed. Therefore, you ought to deliver me; like a frog sitting in a dark well, I am in this world. O Blessed One, you are our refuge; you are our refuge.
Thus ends the first chapter.

Then the Blessed Śākāyanya, being well-pleased, said to the king: "O Great King Bṛhadratha, banner of the Ikṣvāku lineage, you have accomplished your purpose; you are renowned by the name Marut. Which of these, indeed, is your Self? O Blessed One, please describe it. To him he spoke thus. || 1 ||

"That which, having ascended upwards by means of external support, being both trembling and not trembling, dispels darkness—that is the Self," said the Blessed One. Then he said, "That serene being who, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in his own true form—that is the Self; this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. || 2 ||

"Now indeed, O King, this knowledge of Brahman—or rather, the knowledge of all the Upaniṣads—has been explained to us by the venerable Maitreya; I shall relate it to you. Now, there are those known as the Vālakhilyas, who are free from evil, of piercing splendor, and whose vital energy is directed upwards. They once said to Prajāpati: "Venerable Sir, this body is insentient like a cart. Of what being of such a nature—who is beyond the reach of the senses—is this such greatness? By whom has this been established as if it were sentient? Who is its impeller?"

"O Blessed One, tell us this," they said. He spoke to them: "He who is indeed heard to exist above speech—he is this very one who is pure, cleansed, void, tranquil, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the self that is not a lord (*anīśātman*), infinite, imperishable, stable, eternal, unborn, independent, and abides in his own majesty. By him this body is established as if possessed of consciousness, and he is its impeller. They said: "O Blessed One, how is it that by such a one as this—who is desireless—this body is established as if possessed of consciousness?"

"And how is he the impeller of this? To them he said: "That indeed is this subtle one, ungraspable, invisible, designated as the *puruṣa*. With prior intelligence (*buddhipūrva*), it revolves here in this very world by means of a portion (*aṃśa*). Just as one who is asleep is awakened with prior intelligence, so [the *puruṣa*] awakens [the body]. Now, that which is truly its portion is this: the mere consciousness (*cetanamātra*) present in every person, the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), whose characteristics are volition (*saṅkalpa*), determination (*adhyavasāya*), and egoism (*abhimāna*). It is Prajāpati, the all-seeing. By means of that consciousness, this body is established as if it were conscious."

"And he is the impeller of this," they said. "O Blessed One, how can there be a subsistence by a portion for one such as this? He said to them: "In the beginning, Prajāpati alone existed. He found no delight being alone. He meditated upon himself and created many offspring. He saw that these were merely his own self-awakened [projections], breathless, standing like a pillar; he found no delight in them. He thought, 'I shall enter within them to awaken them. Then, having made himself like the wind, he entered within."

Being one, he did not enter; having divided himself fivefold, he is called prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna. Now, that which moves upward is indeed prāṇa; that which moves downward is indeed apāna; that which establishes the coarsest food-essence in the anus and carries the subtlest [essence] equally through every limb is indeed samāna; and that which ejects and swallows what has been drunk and eaten is indeed udāna. Now...

That by which these vessels are pervaded is indeed this *vyāna*. Now, the *upāṃśu* cup overcomes the *antaryāma* cup, and the *antaryāma* cup overcomes the *upāṃśu* cup; in the interval between these two is heat, a fleshy heat. That is the person (*puruṣa*). And that which is the person is Agni Vaiśvānara. It has also been stated elsewhere: "This is Agni Vaiśvānara, who is this infinite person by whom this food is cooked—namely, that which is eaten. Its sound is heard when one covers the ears. When he is about to depart [from the body], [he hears it].

He does not hear this sound. Indeed, he—this very Self—having divided himself fivefold, is placed within the cave; he consists of mind, has vital breath for his body, possesses many forms, and is the Self whose resolve is truth. This very Self, dwelling within his heart, thinking "I have not accomplished my purpose; let me attain my goals," pierced these openings of his and rose up. He eats the objects of the senses through five rays; these which are his rays are the organs of perception (*buddhīndriyāṇi*). His organs of action (*karmendriyāṇi*) are the horses, his chariot is the body, and the mind is the driver.

"Driven by the goad consisting of *prakṛti*, this body indeed revolves like a wheel; yet when dead, this body does not stand up endowed with consciousness. And he is its impeller. (9) "That indeed is the Self (*ātman*). As if led by force, as if overcome by the fruits of actions—both white and black—it moves through various bodies. Because it is unmanifest, subtle, invisible, ungraspable, and free from the sense of 'mine,' it is without fixed abode; though non-acting, it stands as if acting. (10)

Indeed, this [Self] is pure, stable, immovable, untainted, undistracted, free from desire, and stands like a spectator; it remains eating its own food, having concealed itself behind a veil consisting of the qualities (guṇas). Thus it is "established. Thus ends the second chapter.

Indeed, there is another, distinct elemental self (bhūtātman), which, being overwhelmed by the fruits of white and black actions, enters into good and evil wombs; thus, being overwhelmed by pairs of opposites, it wanders along downward or upward paths. This is its detailed explanation: the five subtle elements (tanmātras) are denoted by the word "elements" (bhūta), and the five gross elements (mahābhūtas) are also denoted by the word "elements. Now, that which is their aggregate is called the "body" (śarīra). And that which is indeed called the "body" is—

It has been said that the self is composed of the elements; yet there exists for that [self] another self, like a drop upon a lotus leaf. This very self is overwhelmed by the qualities of *prakṛti*. Because of being thus overwhelmed, it falls into a state of delusion. Due to this lack of non-delusion, it does not perceive the Lord, the Master, the Ordainer who resides within itself. Satiated by the flood of qualities, defiled, unstable, fickle, covetous, distracted, and having fallen into the state of egoism, thinking "I am he" and "this is mine," it binds itself by means of itself.

Just as a bird in the sky, overcome by the fruits of its own actions, wanders about within a net; thus it is said elsewhere: "He who is the agent is indeed this *bhūtātman* (the elemental self), while the inner person (*antar-puruṣa*) is the one who causes [actions] to be performed through the instruments. Now, just as a lump of iron, overcome by fire, attains diversity when struck by smiths, even so, indeed, this *bhūtātman*—overcome by the inner person and struck by the qualities (*guṇas*)—attains diversity. Furthermore, that which consists of the three qualities and has evolved into eighty-four hundred thousand wombs..."

This reality indeed consists of the three qualities; it is the form of manifoldness. These qualities, impelled by the Puruṣa, revolve like a wheel turned by its maker. Just as when a lump of iron is being struck, the fire within it is not overcome, so too that Puruṣa is not overcome; yet this elemental self (bhūtātman) is overcome because of its close attachment [to the qualities]. || 3 ||

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "This body arises solely from sexual intercourse; it is devoid of consciousness, like a pit of excrement as it emerges through the urinary passage. It is built up with bones, smeared with flesh, bound together with skin, and filled with feces, urine, bile, phlegm, marrow, fat, grease, and many other impurities—it is like a decaying chest. (4)

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: delusion, fear, despondency, sleep, lassitude, wounds, old age, grief, hunger, thirst, wretchedness, anger, atheism, ignorance, envy, lack of compassion, folly, shamelessness, deceitfulness, arrogance, and imbalance—these are possessed by one endowed with *tamas*. Thirst, affection, passion, greed, violence, attachment, preoccupation with views, jealousy, lust, instability, restlessness, the desire to take, the acquisition of wealth, and the favoring of friends—[these are possessed by one endowed with *rajas*].

Attachment to objects of the senses is dependence on grasping; aversion toward unpleasant sense-objects and attachment to pleasant ones—this self of beings (bhūtātman), being overwhelmed by these qualities possessed of passion (rājasa), attains various forms; thus it is said, "it attains. || 5 ||

The Fourth Chapter. Then those of sublimated vital energy (ūrdhvaretas), being greatly amazed, gathered together and said: "Venerable sir, homage to you! Teach us; you are our refuge, for no other is known to exist. [They asked: "Who is the guest of this self consisting of the elements (bhūtātman), by whom, having abandoned this world, one attains union with another? He spoke to them as follows.

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "Like waves in great rivers, that which was done by him in the past brings him back; like the tide of the ocean, the arrival of death is difficult to ward off. Bound by snares consisting of good and evil fruits, he is like a tethered animal; like one in captivity, he lacks independence. Like one dwelling in the realm of Yama, he is in a state of manifold fear; like one intoxicated by wine, he is intoxicated by pride; like one seized by a demon, he is driven about; like one bitten by a great serpent, he is afflicted by calamity; and like a great darkness..."

It has been said that this false perception is like a magical illusion for one blinded by passion, like a dream, as insubstantial as the core of a plantain tree, and like an actor’s momentary costume—falsely beautiful like a painted wall. Those objects such as sound, touch, and the rest exist as if they were non-objects; yet the self of beings, being attached to them, does not remember the supreme state. (2)

This indeed is the remedy for the embodied self: the practice of that Dharma which consists in the acquisition of knowledge, proceeding through one's own stages of life (āśramas). One's own duty (svadharma) alone sustains everything, just as the trunk supports the other parts of a tree; by this, one becomes elevated, whereas otherwise one falls downward. He who does not become an ascetic (āśramin) by transgressing his own duty within the Vedas, but remains established in his respective stage of life, is called a "practitioner of austerity" (tapasvin). It has also been said: "There is no attainment of the Self through meditation for one who lacks austerity."

Or it is the purification of karma; for thus he said: "Through austerity, *sattva* is attained; from *sattva*, the mind is fully attained; through the mind, the Self is attained; indeed, by attaining the Self, one ceases [to transmigrate]. (3) In this regard, there are these verses: "Just as a fire without fuel is extinguished in its own source, so the mind, through the cessation of its fluctuations, is extinguished in its own source. (1) "For the mind that has been extinguished in its own source and has gone to the Truth, and for one who is not deluded regarding the objects of the senses, the objects of the senses—following the power of karma—are unreal. (2)

The mind alone is indeed saṃsāra; one should therefore purify it with effort. Whatever the mind is like, that one becomes; this is an eternal secret. (3) By the serenity of the mind, one destroys both auspicious and inauspicious karma. With a serene self, abiding in the Self, one enjoys imperishable happiness. (4) When the mind of a living being is attached to the sphere of sense objects, if it were likewise [attached] to Brahman, who would not be liberated from bondage? (5)

The mind is said to be of two kinds: pure and indeed impure. The impure is characterized by desire and volition; the pure is devoid of desire. (6) Having made the mind perfectly steady, free from both dissolution and distraction, when it reaches the state of non-mind, then that is the supreme state. (7) It should be restrained within the heart until it has reached its dissolution. This alone is knowledge and this is liberation; all else are merely extensive verbal compositions. (8)

The bliss that one obtains when the mind, its impurities shaken off by *samādhi*, is established in the Self—this cannot be described by speech; at that time, it is grasped by the inner organ itself. (9) Just as water does not perceive water, nor fire fire, nor space space within space, so too the person is liberated when the mind has entered within. (10) The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings; attached to sense objects, it leads to bondage; known to be free from sense objects, it leads to liberation. (11)

The Fifth Chapter. Now follows this praise of Kautsāyani: "You are Brahmā, and you indeed are Viṣṇu; you are Rudra, you are Prajāpati. You are Agni, Varuṇa, and Vāyu; you are Indra and you are the Moon. You are Manu and you are Yama; you are the Earth and you are the Imperishable (Acyuta). For the sake of your own self and for the sake of your innate nature, you abide manifoldly in heaven. O Lord of the Universe, salutations to you—the Soul of the Universe and the Maker of all works."

"You are the enjoyer of the universe, the master of universal illusion, the Lord whose delight is in universal play. Salutations to you, the peaceful Self; salutations to the most secret one; and salutations to the inconceivable, the immeasurable, and the one without beginning or end. || 14-15 || 4 ||

This was indeed darkness alone in the beginning. Then, impelled by that which is beyond it, it attains the state of being an object; this is indeed the form of *rajas*. That *rajas*, when impelled, attains the state of inequality; this is indeed the form of *tamas*. That *tamas*, when impelled, flows forth from itself; this is indeed the form of *sattva*. That *sattva*, when impelled, flows forth from itself; that is this portion which is pure consciousness, the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) in each person, characterized by volition, determination, and self-conceit—the Lord of Creatures (*Prajāpati*). His...

The foremost bodies have been declared to be Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu. Now, that which is indeed his *rājasa* portion is this very Brahmā; that which is indeed his *tāmasa* portion is this very Rudra; and that which is indeed his *sāttvika* portion is this very Viṣṇu. He, being one, has become threefold; he has arisen as eightfold, elevenfold, twelvefold, and infinitefold. Because of having arisen, he moves among the beings (*bhūta*).
He has become the support and the overlord of all beings—this Self is both within and without, both within and without. 5.

The Sixth Chapter. This breath indeed sustains itself in two ways: that which is this [breath] and that which is yonder Āditya (the sun). Furthermore, these two paths of his are internal and external; by means of day and night, these two revolve. Yonder Āditya is the external self (*bahirātman*), and the breath is the internal self (*antarātman*). Therefore, by the movement of the external self, the movement of the internal self is inferred. For thus it has been said: "Now, whoever is wise, whose evil is destroyed, who is the overseer of the senses, pure-minded, established in That, and whose gaze is turned inward—he, by the movement of the internal self..."

"The movement of the outer self is inferred," so it has been said. Now, that golden person who is within the sun, who looks down upon this golden earth—he, being established within the lotus of the heart, eats food. || 1 ||

Now, he who dwells within the lotus of the heart and eats food—he is that very fire, the solar one residing in heaven, called Time, invisible, who eats all beings as his food. What is this lotus, and of what is it composed? This lotus is indeed this space; its four quarters and four intermediate directions are situated like petals. These two—the vital breath (Prāṇa) and the Sun—move about within it. One should worship these with the syllable "Om," with the Vyāhṛtis, and with the Sāvitrī verse. || 2 ||

There are indeed two forms of Brahman: the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*). Now, that which is formed is the unreal; that which is formless is the real. That is Brahman; that is the light; that which is the light is the Āditya. This very one became the self (*ātman*) of the syllable *om*. He divided himself threefold: "Om" consists of three morae (*mātrā*); by these, he thought, "I am woven across and through this entire world. For thus it is said: "This Āditya is indeed 'Om'; meditate upon him as such, and yoke yourself to the Self."
Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere: "Now, that which is the Udgītha is the Praṇava; that which is the Praṇava is the Udgītha. "Yonder sun, indeed, is the Udgītha; this [sun] is the Praṇava."

For thus it is said: "One should know the Udgītha, called Praṇava, the leader, whose form is light, free from sleep, free from old age, free from death, three-footed, consisting of three syllables, and again fivefold, hidden in the cave. And thus it is said: "The Brahman with its root above and three feet—the branches are space, air, fire, water, earth, and so forth; this one is named Aśvattha, this is Brahman; its splendor is that which is yonder sun; and this belongs to the syllable Om. Therefore, one should worship this constantly with 'Om'"—this is one [aspect] of it.
Thus, indeed, he says by way of instruction: "This very syllable is meritorious; this very syllable is supreme. Having known this very syllable, whatever one desires, that belongs to him. (4)

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "This body of His is resonant with the syllable *om*; it possesses gender as female, male, and neuter; it is radiant as fire, wind, and the sun; it possesses sovereignty as Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu; it possesses a mouth as the Gārhapatya, Dakṣiṇāgni, and Āhavanīya fires; it possesses discernment as the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman; it possesses the worlds as Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ; it possesses time as the past, present, and future; and it is the vital breath, Agni, and the Sun."

This [syllable] is possessed of majesty, for it obtains food and water; it is possessed of nourishment, for it is the moon; it is possessed of consciousness, for it is intellect, mind, and ego; it is possessed of vital breath, for it is prāṇa, apāna, and vyāna. Thus, when "Om" is uttered, these [powers] are introduced, honored, and established. For thus it has been said: "O Satyakāma, this syllable 'Om' is indeed both the higher and the lower Brahman. || 5 ||

Now, this world was indeed unuttered. That Prajāpati, who is Truth, having performed austerity, uttered it forth: "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. This is the most substantial body of that Prajāpati, namely that which possesses the worlds. Of this [body], "svaḥ" is the head, "bhuvaḥ" is the navel, and "bhūḥ" is the feet. The sun is the eye; for the eye is the great measure of a person, since by means of the eye a person traverses the great measure. Indeed, the eye is truth, for established in the eye, a person moves among all objects.

Therefore, one should worship her as "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. For by this, Prajāpati, the soul of all and the eye of all, becomes worshipped. Thus it is said: "This indeed is the all-sustaining body of Prajāpati; in her all this is contained, and in all this she is contained. Therefore, one should worship her. 6.

Regarding the mantra "Tat Savitur Vareṇyam": the Brahman-knowers say that Savitṛ is indeed the Sun; he is the one who should be chosen for his grace by one who desires the Self. Then, regarding "Bhargo Devasya Dhīmahi": the Brahman-knowers say that Savitṛ is indeed the God; therefore, we meditate upon that which is called his "splendor" (bharga). Then, regarding "Dhiyo Yo Naḥ Pracodayāt": the Brahman-knowers say that "dhīs" are indeed the intellects; [the meaning is] "may he impel our intellects. Then, regarding "Bharga": it is that which is established in yonder Sun, and that which is the pupil in the eye.

This is indeed Bharga; for his movement is by means of light (*bhābhiḥ*), thus he is Bharga; or rather, he is Bharga because he burns (*bharjayati*). Thus say the exponents of Brahman: "Rudra is Bharga. Furthermore, *bha* because he illuminates these worlds; *ra* because he delights these beings; *ga* because these creatures go (*gacchanti*) unto him and come (*āgacchanti*) from him. Therefore, because of his being the refuge (*bhara-gatvāt*), he is Bharga. Because he is eternally generated (*śāśvat sūyamānāt*), he is Sūrya. Because of his impelling (*savanāt*), he is Savitṛ. Because of his eating (*adānāt*), he is Āditya. Because of his purifying (*pavanāt*), he is Pāvana. And because of his nourishing (*āpyāyanāt*), he is Apaḥ. For thus it is said: "He is truly the Self of the Self."

The all-pervading Lord, having entered into the body, is indeed this: the knower, the thinker, the perceiver, the goer, the one who has cast off [the body], the giver of bliss, the doer, the speaker, the taster, the smeller, the seer, the hearer, and the toucher. Thus it is said: "Now, where consciousness has become dualistic, there indeed one hears, sees, smells, tastes, touches, and the Self knows everything. But where consciousness has become non-dualistic—freed from cause, effect, and action, beyond definition, incomparable, and indescribable—what can that be called?"

7. For this indeed is the Self, the Lord, Śambhu, Bhava, Rudra, Prajāpati, the Creator of the universe, Hiraṇyagarbha, Truth, Prāṇa, Haṃsa, the Teacher, Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Arka, Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Samrāj, Indra, and Indu. He who shines there like fire, veiled by fire within a golden egg with a thousand eyes—he indeed is to be desired to be known, he is to be sought after; having granted freedom from fear to all beings, one should go to the forest and then [seek him].

Having cast aside the objects of the senses from his own body, one should perceive him thus: "The omniform, golden-hued Jātavedas, the ultimate refuge, the single light that shines intensely; with a thousand rays existing in a hundred ways, this Sun is the life-breath of all creatures as it rises. || 8 ||

Therefore, this one who knows thus meditates upon the Self alone and sacrifices to the Self alone. Meditation is the mental application during the performance of the rite, praised by the wise. One should purify the mind—which may be defiled by impurity or rendered unclean—by reciting this mantra: "That which is defiled by the remnants of food, or given by a sinner, or [received] from one in a state of birth or death-impurity; may the purifier of Vasiṣṭha, Agni, and the rays of Savitṛ purify my food and whatever other evil there may be. With water, he first surrounds it for the sake of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

He makes five oblations with the [mantras]: "Svāhā to the out-breath (apāna), svāhā to the diffused breath (vyāna), svāhā to the equalizing breath (samāna), svāhā to the up-breath (udāna), svāhā! Then, restraining his speech, he eats what remains. Thereafter, he again covers [the food] from above with water. Having sipped water and become purified, he should meditate upon himself with these two [mantras]: "The breath is Agni; you are the All" and "The breath is Agni, the Supreme Self; indeed, the fivefold wind has taken refuge in him. May he, being pleased, please the All; he is the consumer of the All. You are the All; you are Vaiśvānara; by you the All is supported."
"May all oblations enter you as you are being born; may all creatures be where you are immortal. By this very rite, one indeed returns to the state of being the eater once again. || 9 ||

Furthermore, it should be understood that there is another subsequent modification of this sacrifice to the Self, namely: "the food and the eater of food. Its detailed explanation is as follows: the conscious Person (*puruṣa*) residing within *pradhāna* is the enjoyer; he consumes the food consisting of *prakṛti*. Of him, this elemental self (*bhūtātman*) is indeed the food, and *pradhāna* is its maker. Therefore, that which consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) is the object of enjoyment, while the Person residing within is the enjoyer. In this regard, the proof is "what is seen," because animals originate from seeds; therefore, by this very fact, the seed is the food of *pradhāna*.

The state of being food has been explained; therefore, the Puruṣa is the enjoyer and Prakṛti is the object of enjoyment. Abiding in that [Prakṛti], he enjoys it. Thus, the "food" consisting of Prakṛti—beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas—is that which undergoes transformation through the differentiation of the three Guṇas. By this very [explanation], the fourteen-fold path has been explained. For this world, having become food, is characterized by pleasure, pain, and delusion. Indeed, there is no grasping of sweetness in a seed as long as there is no sprouting; likewise, its state of being food exists in these three stages, beginning with childhood (kaumāra).

Just as youth transforms into old age, so too does the unmanifest (pradhāna) reach the state of manifestation; therein, intellect and the other faculties become "food" consisting of determination, volition, and self-consciousness. Then the objects of the senses become the food for the five [senses]. Thus, all functions of the senses and all functions of the vital breaths [are food]. In this way, the manifest is the food and the unmanifest is the food; its enjoyer is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), and from the fact of being an enjoyer, its consciousness is established. Just as Agni is indeed the eater of food among the gods, so is he.

"Soma is food; by fire alone is food [consumed]. One who knows this thus—that this self, known as Soma, is also known as Agni because of the statement "the Unmanifest is its mouth"—is indeed a person who, through the mouth of the Unmanifest, experiences the three qualities (guṇas). He who knows this is a renunciant (saṃnyāsī), a yogi, and a self-sacrificer (ātmayājī). Furthermore, just as one does not touch women who have entered an empty house, so too he who does not touch the objects of the senses even though they have entered [him] is a renunciant, a yogi, and a self-sacrificer. || 10 ||

Food, indeed, is the supreme form of the self, for this vital breath (*prāṇa*) consists of food. Now, if one does not eat, one becomes a non-thinker, a non-hearer, a non-toucher, a non-feeler, a non-seer, a non-speaker, a non-smeller, and a non-taster, and one gives up the vital breaths. Thus it is said: "But if, indeed, one eats, having become nourished by the vital breath, one becomes a thinker, a hearer, a toucher, a speaker, a taster, a smeller, and a seer. Thus it is said: "From food, indeed, creatures are born—those which..."

Some depend on the earth; therefore they live by food alone, and in the end, they even pass away into it. Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "Indeed, all these beings fall every day toward food, desiring to seize it. The sun takes up the food with its rays; by that [food] he shines. Anointed with food, these vital breaths (prāṇas) digest. Or rather, fire blazes because of food. This world was fashioned by Brahmā out of a desire for food. Therefore, one should meditate upon food as the Self. For thus it says.

"Non-existent things are born; once born, they grow by means of food. It is eaten and it eats beings; therefore, it is called 'food' (anna). (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.2.2) Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "This body which is food is indeed the 'All-Sustainer' (viśvabhṛt), the form of the Blessed Viṣṇu. Breath is the essence of food; mind is the essence of breath; discernment is the essence of mind; and bliss is the essence of discernment. He who knows this becomes possessed of food, possessed of breath, possessed of mind, possessed of discernment, and possessed of bliss—indeed, as far as [these qualities extend] here in this world...

Beings eat food only so long as one who knows this eats the food residing within himself. Food indeed is the conqueror of old age; food is remembered as the means of reconciliation. Food is the life-breath of animals; food is the eldest; food is remembered as the physician. (13)

Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere: "Food is the source of this entire universe, and time is the source of food; the sun is the source of time. Its form is that which is composed of the year consisting of twelve [months], beginning from the *nimeṣa* and other units of time. Half of this [year] belongs to Agni and half to Varuṇa. The half beginning with Maghā up to the middle of Śraviṣṭhā belongs to Agni, while the half beginning with Āśleṣā up to the end of the middle of Śraviṣṭhā belongs to Soma—both in direct and reverse order. Within that, each [constellation] has nine degrees (*navāṃśaka*) of its own, along with the various movements of the planets; because of its subtlety, this is the measure by means of that very [year]."

For time is measured; indeed, there is no apprehension of an object of knowledge without a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Even the object of knowledge attains the status of a means of knowledge through its distinctness, for the purpose of self-awakening. Thus it has been said: "In as many parts as there are of time, in so many does he move who meditates upon time as Brahman; time recedes far away from him. And thus it has been said: "From time all beings flow forth; through time they attain growth; in time they set; time is both the formed and the formless. || 14 ||

There are indeed two forms of Brahman: Time and Non-Time. Now, that which is prior to the sun is Non-Time; it is non-differentiated (akala). But that which begins with the sun is Time; it is differentiated (sakala). This year is indeed the form of the differentiated one. From the year, verily, these creatures are born; by the year they grow once born; in the year they pass away. Therefore, the year is Prajāpati, Time, Food, Brahman, the Nest, and the Self. Thus it is said: "Time ripens all beings."

All these indeed reside within the Great Self (Mahātman). He in whom time is cooked—that one who knows him is a knower of the Veda. This King of Rivers (Sindhu-rāja) is Time personified; he is established among living beings as the one called Savitṛ, from whom these—the moon, the stars, the planets, the years, and so forth—are produced. From them, everything here—whatever good or evil is seen in this world—is derived. Therefore, one should worship the Sun, whose essence is Brahmā, under the name of Time. Some say, "The Sun is Brahmā. Then...
For thus it is said: "The sacrificer, the enjoyer, the oblation, the mantra, the sacrifice, Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, the All, the Indefinite, the Lord, and the Witness—he who shines in that orb. || 16 ||

In the beginning, indeed, this was Brahman alone—endless in the east, endless in the south, endless in the west, endless in the north, endless above and below, and endless in every direction; for in its case, directions such as east and so forth are not applicable, nor are there horizontal, upward, or downward distinctions. This Supreme Self is beyond all measure, inconceivable, and unfathomable; He is the space-self, the one who remains awake even when all else has perished. From this space, He indeed awakens this mere consciousness, and by Him alone is this world meditated upon.

And when this [body] perishes, that radiant form of his—which is the light that shines in yonder sun, in the smokeless fire, and that which is more variegated within the belly, or rather that which digests food—[remains]. For thus it is said: "That which is in the fire, that which is here in the heart, and that which is yonder in the sun—that is this one alone. Indeed, he who knows this attains the oneness of the One. 17.

Likewise, the practice of that [yoga] consists of six limbs: breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), meditation (dhyāna), concentration (dhāraṇā), reasoning (tarka), and absorption (samādhi); this is called yoga. When, by means of this, the seer beholds the golden-hued creator, the Lord, the Puruṣa who is the source of Brahman, then the wise one, having abandoned both merit and sin, unifies everything in the supreme, imperishable state. Thus it is said: "Just as deer and birds do not take refuge on a mountain ablaze with fire, even so faults never take refuge in the knower of Brahman. (18)

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "When indeed the wise man, having restrained the mind externally and having caused the senses to enter into the objects of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), should then remain free from conceptual construction (*niḥsaṅkalpa*). Since the living being known as *prāṇa* has arisen here from that which is beyond *prāṇa*, therefore one should sustain the *prāṇa* within that which is called the Fourth (*turya*)—for thus it is said: 'The thoughtless thought situated in the midst of thought, inconceivable, secret, and supreme; there the mind should be placed, and that sign (*liṅga*) is without support. (19)

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "Therefore, his supreme concentration (*dhāraṇā*)—through the pressing of the palate and the tip of the tongue, and through the restraint of speech, mind, and breath—one perceives Brahman by means of inquiry. When, through the dissolution of the mind, one sees the Self by means of the self as subtler than the subtlest, shining brightly, then, having seen the Self by means of the self, one becomes selfless (*nirātmā*). Being selfless, he is the immeasurable, the unborn, the inconceivable; this is the characteristic of liberation. This is the supreme secret. Thus it is said: "Indeed, by the serenity of the mind, one destroys both auspicious and inauspicious karma."

"Having become serene in soul and abiding in the Self, one attains imperishable bliss. (20) Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "The upward-tending channel called Suṣumṇā is the path for the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). It is severed within the palate. By means of that [channel], joined with the *praṇava* (Oṃkāra) and the mind, one should ascend upwards. Having turned back the tip of the palate and not engaging the senses [with their objects], the Great One should behold the Greatness. Thereafter, he goes beyond the state of having a self; because of being selfless, he does not partake in pleasure or pain, and he attains isolation (*kaivalya*). For thus it has been said:

Having first established the higher [state] and then restrained the breath, one who has crossed to the further shore by means of that which is shoreless should subsequently apply himself to the upward path. Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "There are indeed two Brahmans to be meditated upon: the Word and the Non-word. Now, by the Word alone is the Non-word revealed. Then, therein, the sound 'Om'—having ascended upwards by means of this—attains its dissolution in the Non-word. This, they say, is the goal; this is the immortal; this is union with That (tatsāyujyatvam); this is liberation. And so it is. 21. And thus: And then:

Just as a spider, having ascended upward by means of its thread, gains open space, even so indeed does that meditator, having ascended upward by means of this syllable "Om," attain independence. Otherwise, there are others who maintain the doctrine of sound: through the union of the ear and the thumb, they hear the sound in the space within the heart. This has seven varieties; its analogies are like a river, a small bell, bronze, a wheel, a frog, a bird, and a cricket, or like rain speaking in a windless place. Having transcended that which possesses these distinct characteristics—

When they have set into the Supreme Brahman, which is beyond sound and unmanifest, they become non-distinct in their attributes and non-distinct in their discernment, just as various juices, once combined, attain the state of honey. Thus it is said: "Two Brahmans are to be known: the Śabda-Brahman and that which is the Supreme (Para) Brahman. One who is proficient in the Śabda-Brahman attains the Supreme Brahman. || 22 ||

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "That which is sound is this syllable *oṃ*. That which is its tip is the peaceful, beyond sound, fearless, sorrowless, blissful, satisfied, stable, immovable, immortal, infallible, and eternal, designated as Viṣṇu; for the sake of attaining the state beyond all, one should worship that. Thus it is said: 'That deity who is both supreme and inferior, known by the name Oṃkāra—being beyond sound and having become void—one should practice [meditation] upon him in the location of the crown of the head. || 23 ||

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "The body is the bow, and 'Om' is the arrow; its point is the mind. Having pierced through the darkness characterized by ignorance, one reaches that which is beyond darkness. Then, having pierced through that [darkness], one beholds Brahman—shining like a whirling firebrand, radiant as the sun, full of splendor, and situated beyond the darkness—that which shines in yonder sun, in the moon, in the fire, and in lightning. Indeed, having seen this, one attains immortality. Thus he says: "Meditation is directed inward toward the supreme reality and toward the objects of focus."

It is deposited therein; therefore, non-specific cognition attains the specific. When the mental faculty has dissolved, that bliss which is witnessed by the Self—that is Brahman, the immortal, the pure; that is the goal, and that indeed is the world. || 24 ||

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "He who, with his senses withdrawn in sleep, beholds as if in a dream through an intellect most purified, within the cavity of the senses, the Guide known as *praṇava*—who is of the nature of light, free from sleep, free from old age, free from death, and free from sorrow—he too becomes known as *praṇava*, the Guide, of the nature of light, free from sleep, free from old age, free from death, and free from sorrow. For thus it is said: "In this way, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the syllable *oṃ* [are one], since everything is manifoldly [contained] therein."

Because one joins (*yunakti*) or is joined (*yuñjate*), it is traditionally known as *yoga*. The unification of the vital breath, the mind, and likewise the senses, as well as the renunciation of all states of being, is designated as *yoga*. || 25 ||

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "Just as a fowler, having caught water-birds with a stringed trap, offers them into the fire in his belly, even so, indeed, he offers these vital breaths (*prāṇas*) into the fire of the body by means of this syllable *Om*. Therefore, when the earth is heated, just as clarified butter on the heated earth blazes up upon contact with grass and wood, even so, indeed, this [fire] called 'non-breath' blazes up through contact with the breaths. Now, that which blazes is the form of Brahman, and this is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu."

This indeed is the Rudra-nature of Rudra; having divided himself into immeasurable parts, he thus fills these worlds. For it is said: "Just as sparks indeed issue from fire, and likewise rays from the sun, so too do the vital breaths (prāṇas) and the rest emerge from him here in due order. || 26 ||

Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere: "This heat of the body belongs either to Brahman or to that supreme, immortal, bodiless [Self]; this heat is its clarified butter (ghṛta). Now, being manifest, it is deposited in the sky; thus, with one-pointedness, they pierce the space within the heart, so that it becomes like a light. Therefore, it quickly attains that state, just as an iron mass placed on the ground quickly attains the nature of the earth. Just as blacksmiths and others do not overcome an iron mass when it is situated in clay..."

In this manner, the mind perishes together with its substratum; for thus it is said: "The sheath consisting of the space within the heart is bliss, the supreme abode; from that comes our own yoga, as well as the splendor of both fire and the sun. (27)

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "Having transcended the elements, the senses, and their objects, one should take up the bow whose string is fortitude and whose staff is self-restraint; then, with an arrow consisting of non-conceit, one slays that first gatekeeper of Brahman, who has delusion for his crown, craving and envy for his earrings, sloth for his quiver, and conceit for his supervisor. Then, taking up the bow whose string is desire and whose staff is greed, one slays these very beings with an arrow consisting of will. Having slain him, one crosses to the further shore of the space within the heart by means of the raft of the syllable *Oṃ*."

Having crossed over, when the intermediate space has appeared, he who desires to create the elements slowly enters the pit as if into a pit; thus one should enter the hall of Brahman (*brahmaśālā*). Then, according to the tradition of the Guru, one should push open the four-layered treasury of Brahman (*brahmakośa*). Therefore, [the Self] is pure, cleansed, void, tranquil, breathless, selfless, infinite, imperishable, stable, eternal, unborn, and independent; it abides in its own majesty. Seeing that which abides in its own majesty, one perceives the wheel of movement like a wheel that has ceased to turn. Thus indeed it is said:

But for the embodied one who is disciplined for six months and is constantly liberated, the supreme, infinite, and most secret yoga proceeds perfectly. However, it never occurs for the embodied one who is pierced by passion and darkness, who is intensely inflamed [by worldly desires], and who is attached to children, wife, and family.

Having spoken thus, Śākāyanya vanished within his heart. After offering salutations to him, [the king] said: "O King, by means of this knowledge of Brahman, the sons of Prajāpati have ascended the path of Brahman. Through the practice of yoga, one attains contentment, endurance of the pairs of opposites, and tranquility. This most secret [teaching] should not be proclaimed to one who is not a son, nor to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who is not tranquil; it should be given only to one who is devoted to no other and endowed with all virtues. || 29 ||

"Oṃ! In a pure place, being pure himself, established in goodness (*sattva*), studying the truth, speaking the truth, meditating on the truth, and sacrificing according to the truth—one should become such. Therefore, one who has attained cessation (*nirvṛtti*) regarding the True Brahman, which is the object of true desire, whose bonds are severed by that fruit, and who is free from longing, remains having ascended to imperishable and immeasurable happiness—free from fear toward others as if toward oneself, devoid of desire, and like the extraction of a supreme treasure. Indeed, freedom from desire is the highest extraction of the Supreme.

For that person, consisting of all desires and characterized by determination, volition, and egoism, is bound; therefore, one who is the opposite of that is liberated. Regarding this, some say that the *guṇa* (quality), under the influence of the differentiation of *prakṛti*, undergoes bondage through the nature of determination.

Liberation indeed comes from the destruction of the defects of determination (*adhyavasāya*). For it is by the mind alone that one sees, and by the mind that one hears. Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear—all this is the mind alone. Carried away by the flood of the *guṇas* and rendered turbid, unstable, wavering, being swept away, full of longing, and distracted, it falls into the state of self-conceit (*abhimānitva*). Thinking "I am that" and "this is mine," it thus binds itself by itself, like a bird caught in its own web.

Therefore, the person (puruṣa) is bound when characterized by determination (adhyavasāya), volition (saṅkalpa), and egoism (abhimāna); consequently, one who is the opposite of that is liberated. For this reason, one should remain free from determination, free from volition, and free from egoism—this is the characteristic of liberation. This is the path to Brahman here; this is the opening of the door here, through which one will go to the further shore of this darkness. For all desires are contained herein; regarding this, they cite: "When the five [sensory] cognitions, together with the mind, come to rest..."

When the intellect no longer functions, they call that the supreme goal. Having said this, Śākāyanya vanished; having paid his respects to him and performed the proper rites, he departed for the northern course of the wind, having accomplished his purpose, for there is no movement by a contrary path here. Regarding this, they cite the "Path of Brahman": "Having pierced the solar door, [the rays] emerge upwards. Thus they say: "Infinite are his rays, situated in the heart like a lamp—white, black, brown, blue, tawny, and soft red."

One ray of these stands above; having pierced the solar orb and transcended the world of Brahmā (Brahmaloka), by it they go to the supreme goal. Another hundred rays of his are situated upwards; by them he attains the abodes of the hosts of gods. Those many rays of his which are below, of gentle luster, by means of them he transmigrates downwards for the sake of experiencing karma in this world. Therefore, this blessed Sun is the cause of creation, heaven, and liberation. || 30 ||

"What is the nature of these senses as they function, and who here is their originator and controller? To this he replied: "They have the Self (Ātman) as their essence; for the Self is their originator. Furthermore, there are the Apsarases and the rays called Bhānavīyas. By means of five rays, he consumes the objects of the senses. "Who is the Self? It is that which has been described by characteristics such as being pure, stainless, empty, and tranquil, and which is to be grasped by its own signs. This is the sign of that signless one: namely, the heat inherent in fire and the most auspicious essence of water.

Thus say some. Then others say: speech, hearing, sight, mind, and breath; others say: intellect, fortitude, memory, and wisdom—that is it. Now, these [emanate] from this very one, just as here [on earth] sprouts from a seed, or as smoke, flame, and sparks from fire. Regarding this, they cite: "Just as sparks indeed from a fire, and likewise rays from the sun, so too do the vital breaths and the rest emerge from that here in their respective order. (31)

From this very Self, indeed, all vital breaths, all worlds, all Vedas, all deities, and all beings emerge. Its secret name (*upaniṣad*) is "the Truth of truth. Now, just as when damp wood is placed upon a fire, various clouds of smoke issue forth, even so from this great Being, this has been breathed forth: the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvāṅgirasa, history, ancient lore, sciences, secret names, verses, aphorisms, explanations, and commentaries.

All these beings are indeed its explanations. This Agni is the year consisting of five bricks; its bricks are spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, and winter. It has a head, two wings, a back, and a tail; this Agni is the knower of the person. This is the first layer of Prajāpati. Having lifted the sacrificer with his hands into the intermediate space, he delivered him to Vāyu. Vāyu is indeed breath; Agni is breath. Its bricks are inhalation (*prāṇa*), exhalation (*vyāna*), downward breath (*apāna*), pervasive breath (*samāna*), and upward breath (*udāna*).

He has a head, wings, a back, and a tail; this Agni is man-shaped. This intermediate space is the second layer of Prajāpati; with his hands, he lifted the sacrificer up to heaven and delivered him to Indra. That sun indeed is Indra, and he is this Agni. His bricks are the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, Atharvāṅgirasa, Itihāsa, and Purāṇa. He has a head, wings, a tail, and a back; this Agni is man-shaped. This sky is the third layer of Prajāpati.

With his hands, he makes an offering for the sacrificer to the Knower of the Self, just as the Knower of the Self, having lifted it up, presented it to Brahman; therein he becomes blissful and joyful. The earth is the Gārhapatya fire, the intermediate space is the Dakṣiṇāgni, and the sky is the Āhavanīya. From these very [fires] arise Pavamāna, Pāvaka, and Śuci. By this, his sacrifice is made manifest, since the digestive fire (jāṭhara) is indeed a collection of Pavamāna, Pāvaka, and Śuci. Therefore, Agni is to be sacrificed to, to be piled, to be praised, and to be meditated upon. The sacrificer, having taken the oblation—

He desires meditation upon the deity; he also investigates the meaning of the mantra: "The golden-colored bird, established in the heart and in the sun—the Madgu, the swan, the bull of splendor—him we worship in this fire."

The excellent splendor of that Savitṛ is the object to be meditated upon by him who, dwelling within the intellect as a meditator, pursues here the state of peace of the mind and establishes it in the Self alone. On this subject, there are these verses: 1. Just as a fire without fuel is extinguished in its own source, so the mind, through the cessation of its fluctuations, is extinguished in its own source. 2. For the mind that has been extinguished in its own source and possesses true desire, the objects of the senses—which follow the power of karma and are unreal—become delusive.

3. Mind alone is indeed saṃsāra; one should therefore purify it with effort. Whatever the mind is focused upon, that one becomes; this is the eternal secret. 4. By the serenity of the mind, one destroys both auspicious and inauspicious karma. With a serene self, established in the Self, one enjoys imperishable bliss. 5. If the mind of a living being were as intensely attached to Brahman as it is to the sphere of sense-objects, who would not be liberated from bondage?

6. The mind is said to be of two kinds: pure and impure. It is impure through contact with desire; it is pure when devoid of desire. 7. Having made the mind perfectly steady, free from both dissolution and distraction, when it reaches the state of non-mind, then that is the supreme state. 8. The mind should be restrained within the heart until it comes to an end; this is both knowledge and liberation—the rest are merely elaborations of books.

9. The bliss that arises when the mind, cleansed of impurities by concentration, is established in the Self, cannot be described by speech; at that time, it is apprehended by the inner organ itself. 10. As water in water, fire in fire, or space in space would not be perceived as distinct, so too he whose mind has entered within is fully liberated. 11. The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings; attached to sense objects, it leads to bondage; free from sense objects, it is known as liberation.

Therefore, for those who do not maintain the *agnihotra* fire, who have not built the sacrificial altar (*agni-cit*), and who lack knowledge and contemplation, the recollection of the "Sky of the Brahmin's Foot" is forbidden. Consequently, the Fire must be worshipped, built, praised, and contemplated. 34.

Homage to Agni, who dwells on earth and remembers the world; grant a world to this sacrificer! Homage to Vāyu, who dwells in the intermediate space and remembers the world; grant a world to this sacrificer! Homage to Āditya, who dwells in heaven and remembers the world; grant a world to this sacrificer! Homage to Brahmā, who dwells in all and remembers all; grant everything to this sacrificer! The face of truth is covered by a golden vessel. O Pūṣan, uncover it for Viṣṇu, whose nature is truth, for him who is that [Supreme Being].

The person in the sun—that is indeed I. This is truly the True Dharma (Satyadharma), which is the solar nature (*ādityatva*) of the sun. That white, markless person within the sky is merely a portion of the light that has entered the atmosphere; this is what is in the center of the sun, as it were. This is in the eye and in the fire. This is Brahman; this is the Immortal; this is Bharga. This is the True Dharma, a mere portion of the light that has entered the atmosphere; this is the Immortal in the center of the sun, of which Soma is the sprout and the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are the roots.

This is Brahman; this is the Immortal; this is Bharga. This is the True Dharma, a mere fraction of the splendor situated within the ether. It is that which shines as the Yajus in the midst of the sun—Omāp, jyotis, rasa, amṛta, brahma, bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, Om.

The pure swan with eight feet, possessing three threads, subtle and imperishable, blind to dualities yet kindled by splendor—he who sees all sees this: that which is but a minute portion of the splendor situated within the sky, which, having risen in the midst of the sun, becomes two rays; this is Savitṛ, this is the True Dharma, this is the Yajus, this is austerity, this is Agni, this is Vāyu, this is Prāṇa, this is water, this is the moon, this is the bright, this is the immortal, this is the sphere of Brahman, this is the light-ocean; in that very ocean is the sacrificer, like a lump of salt.

They seem to dissolve away; this indeed is the oneness with Brahman, for here all desires are contained. Regarding this they cite: "Like a stream of liquid stirred by a subtle breeze, that which dwells within the gods quivers. He who knows thus is a knower of the All, he is a knower of duality, and he should be one whose light is unified and whose nature is that [Brahman]. Those drops which rise up incessantly like lightning from the glow of clouds in the highest heaven—they are indeed the rays of glory, appearing as if with matted locks due to their dwelling in the abode of fame, like the flames of the black-pathed fire. (35)

Indeed, there are two forms of the Brahman-light: one is the tranquil (*śānta*) and one is the prosperous (*samṛddha*). Now, that which is tranquil has space (*kha*) as its support; and that which is prosperous has this [world] as its food. Therefore, one should sacrifice within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*) with mantras, herbs, clarified butter, meat, sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), cooked offerings (*sthālīpāka*), and so forth, and with the remnants of food and drink remaining on the hearth (*āsnya*); regarding the Āhavanīya fire, one should think, "For the prosperity of splendor, for the sake of conquering the world of merit, and for immortality. On this point they cite: "One who desires heaven should offer the Agnihotra."

One attains the realm of Yama by means of the Agniṣṭoma, the realm of Soma by means of the Uktha, the realm of the Sun by means of the Ṣoḍaśin, sovereignty by means of the Atirātra, and the realm of Prajāpati by means of a sacrifice lasting up to a thousand years. Just as the stability of a lamp depends on the wick, the fuel, and the oil, so too do these two [the individual soul and the cosmic egg] abide through their internal application to the Self and the Egg of the World. || 36 ||

Therefore, one should worship this immeasurable splendor with the syllable *om*. It is declared to be threefold: in fire, in the sun, and in the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Now, this channel called "abundance of food" carries what is offered into the fire toward the sun; from that, the essence which flowed down rains as the *udgītha*. By that, these vital breaths exist, and from the vital breaths, living beings arise. Regarding this, they cite an example: "The oblation that is poured into the fire, that it causes to go to the sun; the sun rains by means of its rays; thereby food comes into being; from food, the origin of all beings. For thus it is said: "In the fire..."

The oblation properly offered reaches the sun; from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings. By performing the *agnihotra* sacrifice, one pierces the net of greed; then, having cut through delusion, no longer praising anger, and contemplating desire, one pierces the four-layered sheath of Brahman. From there, having pierced the spheres of the sun, the moon, fire, and the quality of goodness (*sattva*), one becomes pure and [reaches] the immovable, immortal, and infallible [state] situated within the essence of being.

One beholds that which is certainly named Viṣṇu, the supreme abode of all, endowed with true desire and omniscience, independent consciousness abiding in its own glory. Regarding this, they cite: "The moon resides in the midst of the sun; fire resides in the midst of the moon; the principle of existence (sattva) resides in the midst of light; and the Imperishable (Acyuta) resides in the midst of existence."

Having meditated on the connection of the body, the span of a thumb, and even the atom, one attains the state beyond this, for "all desires are contained herein. Regarding this, they cite: "The Great God, whose body is the size of a thumb-span, entered the worlds in three ways, like the spreading heat of a lamp; that Brahman is praised with the syllable Om. Om! Salutations to Brahman! Salutations! Thus ends the sixth chapter.

Prapāṭhaka 7. Agni, the Gāyatra, the Trivṛt, the Rathantara, the spring, the vital breath, the stars, and the Vasus rise in the east; they heat, they rain, they praise, and they withdraw again. They look within the interstices. He is inconceivable, formless, profound, the enjoyer of qualities, beyond dissolution, the Lord of Yoga, omniscient, generous, immeasurable, without beginning or end, glorious, unborn, wise, indefinable, the creator of all, the Self of all, the consumer of all, the ruler of all, and the innermost within all. 1.

Indra, the Triṣṭubh meter, the Pañcadaśa-stoma, the Bṛhat-sāman, the summer season, the Vyāna-vital breath, Soma, and the Rudras rise from the south; they heat, rain, praise, and again enter [the world]. They look through the internal aperture—he who is without beginning or end, immeasurable, undivided, not dependent on another, independent, signless, formless, possessed of infinite power, the Ordainer, the Maker of Light. || 2 ||

The Maruts, the Jagatī meter, the seventeenfold Stoma, the Vairūpa Sāman, the rainy season, the Apāna breath, and the Śukra [cup]—the Ādityas rise in the west, they heat, they rain, they praise, and they enter again; through the internal aperture they look out. That is the most peaceful, soundless, fearless, sorrowless, blissful, satisfied, steady, immovable, immortal, infallible, eternal state known as Viṣṇu, the ultimate abode of all. || 3 ||

The Viśvedevas are the Anuṣṭubh meter, the twenty-one-fold Stoma, the Vairāja Sāman, and the autumn season; Varuṇa and the Sādhyas rise up from the north, they heat, they rain, they praise, and they enter again. Within the opening, they look; within, he is pure, cleansed, void, peaceful, breathless, selfless, and infinite. 4.

Mitra and Varuṇa; the Paṅkti, Triṇava, and Trayastriṃśa meters; the Śākvara and Raivata Sāmans; the winter and the cool season; the upward vital breath (udāna); the Aṅgirasas; and the Moon—these rise upwards, they heat, they rain, they praise, and they enter again. Through the internal aperture, they behold the one called Praṇava, the leader, whose form is light, who is free from sleep, free from old age, free from death, and free from sorrow. || 5 ||

Saturn, Rāhu, Ketu, serpents, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, humans, birds, Śarabhas, elephants, and others rise up from below, scorch, rain down, praise, and again enter; they look through the internal cavity [of him] who is the wise sustainer, the innermost of all, imperishable, pure, purified, radiant, patient, and tranquil. || 6 ||

For this very Self within the heart is subtler than a firefly, yet like a kindled fire, it is multiformed; all this is its food, and upon it these creatures are woven. This is the Self, free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from doubt, free from hunger, whose resolve is true, whose desires are true. He is the Supreme Lord, the Sovereign of beings, the Protector of beings, the Bridge, the Sustainer. For he indeed is the Self, the Ruler, Śambhu, Bhava, Rudra, Prajāpati, the Creator of the universe, Hiraṇyagarbha, Truth, and Breath.

The Haṃsa, the Praśasta, Acyuta, Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa—he who is in the fire, he who is here in the heart, and he who is yonder in the sun, he is this one alone. Homage to you, that one of universal form, established in the true ether. || 7 ||

Now, O King, these are the obstacles to knowledge; this is indeed the source of the snare of delusion: that people cling to what is beneath them even when the gateway to heaven has been described before them by those who do not themselves go to heaven. Furthermore, there are others who are constantly merry, constantly traveling, constantly begging, and constantly living by their crafts; and others who are city-beggars, beggars for whom one should not sacrifice, disciples of Śūdras, and Śūdras who are learned in the scriptures; and yet others who are flatterers, matted-hair ascetics, actors, soldiers, wandering mendicants, and performers on the stage.

Those who are engaged in royal service, those who claim, "We pacify the afflictions caused by Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, hosts of Bhūtas, Piśācas, Uragas, Grahas, and others," as well as those others who wear saffron robes and earrings in vain, the Kāpālikas, and those others who, through false logic, fallacies, trickery, and sorcery, seek to stand as opponents among the followers of the Veda—they should not dwell with such people. For they are like thieves who have become manifest; they do not lead to heaven. Thus it has been said:

8. The world, being deluded by the deceivers who preach selflessness (*nairātmya*) through false examples and reasons, does not know that which is the other branch of Vedic knowledge. Indeed, Bṛhaspati, having become Śukra, created this ignorance for the sake of Indra’s fearlessness and for the destruction of the Asuras. By means of it, they designate the auspicious as inauspicious and the inauspicious as auspicious; they say, "Let there be meditation on the dharma that destroys the Vedic scriptures and other treatises. Therefore, one should not speak of this [ignorance], for otherwise it is like a barren woman; its fruit is merely sensual pleasure.

"One who has fallen from right conduct should not even be approached," for thus it is said: "Far apart and leading in opposite directions are these two: ignorance and that which is known as knowledge. I consider Naciketas to be a seeker of knowledge; many desires do not entice you. He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together—having crossed over death by means of ignorance, he enjoys immortality through knowledge. Enveloped within ignorance, yet considering themselves wise and learned..."

Wandering about, the deluded go around like blind men led by one who is himself blind. Indeed, the gods and the asuras, desiring the Self, went into the presence of Brahmā. Having paid homage to him, they said: "O Blessed One, we desire the Self; please tell it to us. Then, having meditated for a long time, he thought: "These asuras are indeed of a different nature; therefore, let something other [than the truth] be told to them. Thus, these deluded ones subsist upon that which was spoken to them—clinging to it, striking down the crossing point, proclaiming falsehood as if it were truth.

"Seeing [the world] as if it were a magician's trick—therefore, that which is declared in the Vedas is the truth; what is spoken in the Vedas is what the wise rely upon. For this reason, a Brahmin should not study anything non-Vedic; such is the meaning. (10)

Indeed, this is the true nature of that sky which is contained within the void: it is the supreme light, which is declared to be threefold—in fire, in the sun, and in the vital breath (prāṇa). Indeed, this is the true nature of that sky which is contained within the void: it is this syllable "Om. By means of this alone, one awakens from it, rises up from it, and breathes forth; for the intellect of Brahman has this as its constant support. Here, in this very atmosphere of the sky, having climbed up by way of the branches, one moves from joint to joint, like one who casts salt into water or ghee.

Regarding this, they cite the following: "It is like the heat of one who is feverish; it is like its expansion. Now, why is it called *vaidyuta* (the lightning-like)? Because as soon as it is uttered, it illuminates the entire body; therefore, one should worship this with the syllable *Om* as immeasurable splendor. 1. This person who resides in the right eye is Indra; his wife resides in the left eye. 2. Their union occurs within the hollow of the heart.

The essence of that blood here is indeed a mass of both of them. From the heart it comes forth; it is established in the eye. That channel of theirs is a conduit, being one yet divided into two for the two [organs]. It strikes the bodily fire of the mind, which impels the vital air (māruta). Moving within the chest, the vital air produces a deep tone. Through the union of the churning-stick and the fire in the heart, the subtle atom (aṇu) becomes twice as subtle (dviraṇu) in the region of the throat.

Know that at the tip of the tongue there is a triad of atoms (tryaṇuka) which has emerged; thus they speak of the Mātṛka. One who does not see death sees neither disease nor suffering. For seeing everything, one sees all and attains everything in every way. The visual, the dream-walker, the sleeper, and that which is beyond sleep—these are its four divisions, and among them, the fourth is the greatest. One may move with one foot in the [first] three, and one moves with three feet in the higher [state].

"The duality of the Great Self exists for the purpose of experiencing truth and untruth. Thus [ends the statement], "The duality of the Great Self. Thus ends the seventh chapter. Om. May they swell—thus [is] the peace mantra. Thus the Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad is complete.

The Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad Now begins the Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad, a general Upaniṣad belonging to the Sāmaveda. I am that Great Splendor, the state of the Triple-foot (tripada) which sages attain through the awakening to Brahman alone, accompanied by devotion arising from dispassion. Om! May my limbs, speech, breath, eye, ear, as well as strength and the senses, grow strong.

May all things be the Upanishad of Brahman; may I not reject Brahman, nor may Brahman reject me. May there be non-rejection, may there be non-rejection for me. May those qualities which are in the Upanishads abide in me who is devoted to the Self; may they abide in me. Om! Peace! Peace! Peace! The Maitrāyaṇī, Kauṣītaki, Bṛhajjābāla, Tāpanī, Kālāgnirudra, Maitreyī, Subāla, Kṣurikā, and Mantrikā.

Oṃ. There was once a king named Bṛhadratha. Having entrusted his kingdom to his eldest son and considering this world to be impermanent, he attained a state of detachment from the body and departed for the forest. There, having undertaken supreme austerity, he stood with his arms upraised, gazing at the sun. At the end of a thousand years, a sage approached him—one who was like smokeless fire, as if burning with splendor, the venerable Śākāyanya, a knower of the Self. He said to the king, "Arise, arise! Choose a boon. To him...

Having paid homage, he said: "O Blessed One, I am not a knower of the Self; you are a knower of reality. We have heard of you; therefore, please speak to us. [Śākāyanya replied: "This was requested by me previously, but it is impossible. Do not ask this question, O descendant of Ikṣvāku; choose other boons. While being touched on his feet by Śākāyanya, the king uttered this verse: 1. "The gods indeed concealed from me this Brahman, which is easy to perceive and near at hand. It does not shine forth for one who is deluded by wealth and overcome by pride, thinking 'I am wealthy' and 'I am successful. || 1 ||

O Blessed One, in this body—which is defiled by bone, skin, sinew, marrow, flesh, semen, blood, phlegm, tears, feces, urine, wind, bile, and phlegm; which is foul-smelling, unsubstantial, and a mere conglomeration—what is the use of the enjoyment of sensual pleasures? (2) In this body—which is assailed by desire, anger, greed, fear, despair, envy, separation from the beloved, union with the unpleasant, hunger, thirst, old age, death, disease, grief, and so forth—what is the use of the enjoyment of sensual pleasures? (3)

And we see that all this is perishable, just as these gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like, which perish like blades of grass, are subject to arising and destruction. Now, what of these others—those other great archers and universal monarchs (cakravartins), such as Sudyumna, Bhūridyumna, Indradyumna, Kuvalayāśva, Yauvanāśva, Śvāśvapati, Śaśabindu, Hariścandra, Ambarīṣa, Yayāti, Naraṇyu, Ukṣasena, Uthamarutta, Bharata, and so forth? Even as they were being watched... [they perished].* *Note: The sentence appears to be incomplete in the source text.*

Having abandoned the great prosperity of their circle of kinsmen, they depart from this world for that other world. (5) Moreover, what need is there to mention others? We observe the cessation [of suffering] even for Gandharvas, Asuras, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, hosts of Bhūtas, Piśācas, Uragas, Grahas, and so forth. (6)

Now, what is the use of these enjoyments of desire in this kind of saṃsāra—where there is the drying up of other great oceans, the falling of mountains, the shaking or the shifting of the pole star, the sinking of trees, and the displacement of the earth from its place, as well as the gods themselves? For one who has resorted to these, repeated wandering here is observed. Therefore, you ought to deliver me; O Blessed One, I am like a frog sitting in a dark well in this saṃsāra. You are our refuge; you are our refuge.
Thus ends the first chapter.

Then the Blessed Śākāyanya, being well-pleased, said to the king: "O Great King Bṛhadratha, you are the banner of the Ikṣvāku lineage, the foremost among the sons; you have accomplished all that was to be done and are renowned by the name Marut. Which of these, indeed, is your Self? O Blessed One, please describe it. To him he spoke thus. || 1 ||

"That which, having ascended upwards by means of external support, being both trembling and not trembling, dispels darkness—that is the Self," said the Blessed One. Then he said, "That serene being who, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in his own true form—that is the Self; this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. || 2 ||

"Now then, O King, this knowledge of Brahman—or rather, the knowledge of all the Upaniṣads—has been explained to us by the venerable Maitreya; I shall relate it to you. Now, there are those known as the Vālakhilyas, who are free from evil, of piercing splendor, and whose vital energies are directed upward. They once said to Prajāpati: "Venerable Sir, this body is insentient like a cart. To whom indeed belongs such greatness, belonging to one who has transcended the senses, by whom this [body] is established as if it were sentient? Who is its impeller?"

"O Blessed One, tell us this," they said. He spoke to them: "He who is indeed heard of as being above speech—he is this very one who is pure, cleansed, void, peaceful, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the self that is not a lord (*anīśātman*), infinite, imperishable, stable, eternal, unborn, independent, and abides in his own majesty. By him this body is established as if possessed of consciousness, and he is its impeller. They said: "O Blessed One, how is it that by such a one as this—who is without desire—this [body] is established as if possessed of consciousness?"

"And how is he the impeller of this [body]?"—to them he said: "Verily, that one is subtle, ungraspable, invisible, designated as the *puruṣa*; with prior intelligence (*buddhipūrva*), he revolves here by means of a portion (*aṃśa*) even while one is in deep sleep. With prior intelligence, he awakens him, as it were. Now, that which is indeed his portion is this which consists of mere consciousness (*cetanamātra*); for every person, it is the *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field), characterized by volition, determination, and self-conceit (*abhimāna*). It is Prajāpati, the all-seeing; by that consciousness, this body is established as if possessed of consciousness."

"And he is the impeller of this [body]," they said. "O Blessed One, how can there be a functioning by means of a portion for one such as this? He said to them: "In the beginning, Prajāpati alone existed. He did not find delight being alone. He meditated upon himself and created many creatures. He saw that these were merely his own self-awakened forms, breathless and standing like a pillar; he did not find delight in them. He thought, 'I shall enter within them to awaken them. Then, having made himself like the wind, he entered within."

Being one, he did not enter; having divided himself fivefold, he is called Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, Udāna, and Vyāna. Now, that which moves upward is indeed Prāṇa; and that which moves downward is indeed Apāna; and that which establishes the coarsest food-essence in the Apāna and leads the subtlest [essence] equally to every limb is indeed Samāna; and that which vomits up and swallows what has been drunk and eaten is indeed Udāna; and now...
