He does not hear this sound. Indeed, this very Self, having divided itself fivefold and being established in the cave, consists of mind, has vital breath for its body, possesses many forms, and is the Self whose resolve is truth. This very Self, dwelling within his heart, thinking "I have not accomplished my purpose; I shall attain my goals," pierced these openings and emerged with five rays; it eats the objects of sense through these five rays, which are the organs of perception. These which are its rays are the organs of action; its chariot is the body, and the mind is the driver.

"Driven by the goad of its own material nature (*prakṛti*), this body indeed revolves like a wheel; yet when dead, this body does not remain established as if possessed of consciousness. And he is its impeller. (9) "That indeed is the Self (*ātman*). As if led by force, as if overcome by the fruits of actions—both white and black—it moves through various bodies. Because it is unmanifest, subtle, invisible, ungraspable, and free from the sense of 'mine,' it is without fixed location; though non-doing, it stands as if it were the doer. (10)

Indeed, this [Self] is pure, firm, immovable, untainted, undisturbed, free from longing, and stands like a spectator; it remains with its own conduct concealed by a veil consisting of the qualities (guṇas), thus it is said to be "established. Thus ends the second chapter.

They said, "O Blessed One, if you thus indicate the majesty of this Self, then who is this other, supreme Self, that—overwhelmed by the fruits of white and black actions—attains good and evil wombs, and being overwhelmed by dualities, wanders about in a downward or upward course? Which one is this? To them he spoke. || 1 ||

Indeed, there is another, distinct elemental self (*bhūtātman*), which—overwhelmed by the fruits of white and black actions—enters into good and evil wombs, wandering about, overwhelmed by pairs of opposites, through upward or downward courses. This is its detailed explanation: the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are denoted by the word "element" (*bhūta*), and the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*) are also denoted by the word "element. Now, that which is their aggregate is called the "body" (*śarīra*); and that which was indeed said to be the body is this [self].

It has been said that the self is composed of the elements (bhūtātman). Now, there exists a Self of that [elemental self], like a drop upon a lotus leaf. This very [elemental] self is overwhelmed by the qualities of primordial nature (prākṛta-guṇa); because of this state of being overwhelmed, it falls into a state of delusion. Due to its lack of non-delusion, it does not perceive the Lord, the Master, the Ordainer who resides within itself. Being satisfied by the flood of qualities, it becomes defiled, unstable, fickle, greedy, and distracted; having fallen into the state of egoism, thinking "I am he" and "this is mine," it binds itself by means of itself.

"Like a bird caught in a net, being overcome by the fruits of its own actions, it wanders about. Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "He who is the agent is indeed this *bhūtātman* (the elemental self); the inner person (*antar-puruṣa*) is the one who causes [actions] to be performed through the instruments [of the senses]. Now, just as an iron ball, overcome by fire, assumes various forms when struck by smiths, even so indeed this *bhūtātman*, overcome by the inner person and struck by the qualities (*guṇas*), assumes various forms. And that which consists of the three qualities and has evolved into eighty-four hundred thousand wombs..."

This indeed consists of the three real qualities (*guṇa*); it is the form of manifoldness. These qualities, impelled by the Person (*puruṣa*), move like the wheel [is moved] by the wheelwright. Just as when a lump of iron is being struck, the fire within it is not overcome, so too that Person is not overcome; but this elemental self (*bhūtātman*) is overcome because of its close attachment [to the qualities]. || 3 ||

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "This body arises solely from sexual intercourse; it is devoid of consciousness, like a mere pit, emerging through the urinary passage; it is built up with bones, smeared with flesh, bound together with skin, and filled with feces, urine, bile, phlegm, marrow, fat, grease, and many other impurities—it is like a decaying sheath. (4)

Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere: delusion, fear, despondency, sleep, lassitude, wounds, old age, grief, hunger, thirst, wretchedness, anger, atheism, ignorance, envy, lack of compassion, stupidity, shamelessness, deceitfulness, arrogance, and imbalance—these are possessed by one endowed with *tamas*. Thirst, affection, passion, greed, violence, attachment, preoccupation with views, jealousy, lust, instability, fickleness, the desire to steal, the acquisition of wealth, and the favoring of friends—[these are possessed by one endowed with *rajas*].

Attachment to objects of the senses is clinging; aversion toward unpleasant sense-objects and infatuation with pleasant ones—this self of beings (*bhūtātman*), being overwhelmed by these qualities filled with passion (*rājasa*), attains various forms; thus it is said, "it attains. (3.5) The Third Chapter.

Then, indeed, those whose vital energies were drawn upward (the *ūrdhvaretas*), being greatly amazed, approached him closely and said: "Venerable sir, salutations to you! Teach us; you are our refuge, for no other is found. Who is this guest of the self (*bhūtātman*) by whom, having abandoned this [body], one attains union (*sāyujya*) with another? He spoke to them as follows. || 1 ||

Moreover, it is said elsewhere: his past deeds turn him back like waves in great rivers; the arrival of death is as unavoidable as the tide of the ocean. Bound by the snares consisting of the fruits of good and evil, he is like a tethered animal; like one held in captivity, he lacks independence; like one situated in the realm of Yama, he is in a state of manifold fear; like one intoxicated by wine, he is intoxicated by the intoxication of pride; like one seized by a demon, he is driven about; like one bitten by a great serpent, he is afflicted by calamity; and like a great darkness...

Blinded by passion, it is like a magical illusion, consisting of delusion, and like a false dream; it is as pithless as the core of a plantain tree, and like an actor, its appearance is momentary; it is as falsely pleasing as a painted wall—thus it has been said. Those objects such as sound, touch, and the rest exist as if they were non-objects; yet the individual soul, being attached to them, does not remember the supreme state.

Indeed, this is the remedy for the embodied soul: the practice of the Dharma acquired through knowledge, proceeding according to one's own stages of life (*āśrama*). One's own duty (*svadharma*) alone supports everything, just as the trunk supports the other branches; by this, one moves upward, whereas otherwise one falls downward. He who is overcome by his own duty is not truly established in the Vedas. One who does not transgress his own duty while remaining within the stages of life is called an ascetic (*tapasvin*); for it has been said that there is no attainment of self-meditation for one who lacks austerity.

Or rather, it is the purification of action; for thus it has been said: "Through austerity, *sattva* is attained; from *sattva*, the mind is attained; through the mind, the Self is attained; and by attaining the Self, one ceases [from rebirth]. (3) In this regard, there are these verses: "Just as a fire without fuel is extinguished in its own source, so the mind, through the cessation of its fluctuations, is extinguished in its own source. (1) "For the mind that has been extinguished in its own source, which moves toward truth and is no longer deluded by the objects of the senses, the objects of the senses—falsely perceived and following the power of karma—cease to exist. (2)

The mind alone is indeed saṃsāra; one should purify it with diligent effort. Whatever the mind is, that one becomes—that is the eternal secret. (3) By the serenity of the mind, one destroys both auspicious and inauspicious karma. With a serene self, abiding in the Self, one enjoys imperishable happiness. (4) When the mind of a living being is intensely attached to the sphere of sense objects, if it were likewise so toward Brahman, who would not be liberated from bondage? (5)

The mind is said to be of two kinds: pure and indeed impure. The impure is characterized by desire and volition; the pure is devoid of desire. (6) Having made the mind perfectly steady, free from both dissolution and distraction, when it reaches the state of non-mind, that is the supreme state. (7) It should be restrained within the heart until it has reached its dissolution. This is both knowledge and liberation; all else are merely extensive elaborations of books. (8)

The bliss that one attains when the mind—its impurities shaken off by *samādhi* and established in the Self—is then impossible to describe with words; it is grasped by the inner organ itself. (9) Just as water does not perceive water, nor fire within fire, nor space within space, so too the person is liberated when the mind has entered within. (10) The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings. Attached to sense objects, it leads to bondage; known to be free from sense objects, it leads to liberation. (11)

Now, this is the praise by Kautsāyani: "You are Brahmā, and you are indeed Viṣṇu; you are Rudra, you are Prajāpati. You are Agni, Varuṇa, and Vāyu; you are Indra, you are the Moon. You are Manu, you are Yama; you are the Earth, and you are the Infallible (Acyuta). For your own sake and for the sake of your innate nature, you abide manifoldly in heaven. O Lord of the Universe, salutations to you, the Soul of the Universe, the Maker of all works."

You are the enjoyer of the universe, the one whose very nature is the universe, the Lord who delights in universal play. Salutations to you, the peaceful self; salutations to the most secret one; and salutations to the inconceivable, the immeasurable, and the one without beginning or end. || 14–15 || 4.4 ||

This was indeed darkness alone in the beginning; thereafter, impelled by that [darkness], it attains the state of being an object—this is indeed the form of *rajas*. That *rajas*, when impelled, attains the state of inequality—this is indeed the form of *tamas*. That *tamas*, when impelled, flows forth from itself—this is indeed the form of *sattva*. That *sattva*, being impelled, flows forth from itself; this is that portion which is pure consciousness, the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) in each person, characterized by volition, determination, and self-conceit—the Lord of Creatures (*Prajāpati*). His...

The foremost bodies have been declared to be Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu. Now, that which is indeed his *rājasa* portion is this very Brahmā; that which is indeed his *tāmasa* portion is this very Rudra; and that which is indeed his *sāttvika* portion is this very Viṣṇu. This one, being thus threefold, has arisen as eightfold, elevenfold, twelvefold, and infinitefold. Because he has arisen, he moves among the beings as their foundation.
"He became the lord of all beings"—thus [it is said that] this Self is both within and without, and within and without. The Fourth Chapter.

This one indeed sustains himself in two ways: that which is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and that which is yonder sun (*āditya*). Now, these two were originally one, but they became fivefold by name: internally and externally, as day and night; these two revolve. Yonder sun is the external self (*bahirātman*), while the vital breath is the internal self (*antarātman*); the external self is inferred through the movement of the internal self.

"Movement"—thus indeed it is said. Whosoever is wise, free from evil, the overseer, pure-minded, established in That, with eyes turned inward—he, having reached the inner self, infers the outer self; "movement"—thus indeed it is said. Now, that golden person who is within the sun, who beholds me as golden—he is this very one who, resting within the lotus of the heart, eats food. || 1 ||

Now, he who dwells within the lotus of the heart and eats food—he is that very fire, the solar one situated in heaven, called Time, invisible, who eats the food of all beings. What is this lotus? Does he know it? Indeed, that lotus is this space; its four quarters, the four intermediate directions, and their junctions are its petals. This fire is on this side, while beyond it are these two: Prāṇa and Āditya. One should worship these two with the syllable *om*, with the *vyāhṛtis*, and with the *Sāvitrī*. Thus ends the second section.

There are indeed two forms of Brahman: the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*). Now, that which is formed is the unreal; that which is formless is the real. That which is the real is Brahman; that which is Brahman is light; that which is light is the Āditya. This very one is the Self (*ātman*) consisting of the syllable *om*. He divided himself threefold. The syllable *om* has three measures (*mātrā*); by these all this [universe] is woven across and lengthwise. Thus it is said: "One should meditate upon the Āditya as *om*, and thus one should yoke the Self. 3.

Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere: "Now, that which is the Udgītha is the Praṇava; that which is the Praṇava is the Udgītha. This very Sun is the Udgītha and the Praṇava. For thus it has been said: "The Udgītha is to be known as fivefold—the one called Praṇava, the Leader, Name-and-Form, the Sleepless, the Ageless, and the Deathless—hidden in the cave of the heart. And thus it has been said: "With its root above and branches extending down to Brahmā, consisting of ether, air, fire, water, earth, and so forth—all this is consumed by the One; this is Brahman, and this is its essence, namely, this Sun."

"This is the meaning of this syllable *om*; therefore, one should worship this [Brahman] continuously with this [syllable]. This is one way to make known its essence. Thus he said: "This very syllable is meritorious; having known this very syllable, whatever one desires, that belongs to him. || 4 ||

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "This [syllable Om] is his body that thunders; it possesses gender, being female, male, and neuter; it possesses radiance, being fire, wind, and the sun; it possesses sovereignty, being Rudra and Viṣṇu; it possesses a mouth, being the Gārhapatya, Dakṣiṇāgni, and Āhavanīya fires; it possesses discernment, being the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman; it possesses worlds, being Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svar; it possesses time, being the past, present, and future; and it is breath, fire, and the sun."

"This [syllable] is possessed of majesty, for it is food, water, and the moon; this is possessed of nourishment; this is possessed of consciousness, for it is intellect, mind, and ego; this is possessed of vital breath, for it is the out-breath, the in-breath, and the diffused breath—so say some. When one says 'I renounce,' it is said that these are surrendered to the Prastotṛ. For thus it has been said: 'O Satyakāma, this syllable "Om" is indeed both the higher and the lower.'"

Now, this was indeed opened up; Prajāpati, having performed austerity, uttered it: *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. This, indeed, is the most substantial body of Prajāpati, the one possessing worlds (*lokavatī*). Of this [body], *svaḥ* is the head, *bhuvaḥ* is the navel, and *bhūḥ* is the feet. The Sun is fixed as the eye of the Great Puruṣa; for by means of the eye, this person moves through measures (*mātrā*). The eye is indeed truth, for when established in the eyes, a person speaks regarding all matters. Therefore, one should meditate upon *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, for it is food.

"Prajāpati, the soul of all, becomes worshipped as if he were the eye of the universe. For thus it is said: "This indeed is Prajāpati’s body that sustains all; in this [body] everything is contained, and in everything this [body] is contained. Therefore, one should worship this. || 6 ||

Regarding the verse "Tat savitur vareṇyam" (That excellent glory of Savitṛ): Savitṛ is indeed the Sun; the knowers of Brahman say that he is thus to be chosen by one who desires the Self. Then, regarding "Bhargo devasya dhīmahi" (We meditate on the glory of the God): Savitṛ is indeed established in those [heavenly lights]; the knowers of Brahman say, "Which of his glories shall we contemplate? Then, regarding "Dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt" (Who may inspire our thoughts): "Thoughts" (dhiyaḥ) are indeed the intellects; the knowers of Brahman say, "He who may inspire these thoughts of ours. Then, regarding "Bharga": it is that which is placed within this Sun, within the pupil of the eye.

This is called Bharga; for his movement is by means of radiance (*bhās*), thus he is Bharga; indeed, he burns (*bharjati*), thus he is Bharga—so say the exponents of Brahman. Furthermore, "Bharga" because he illuminates these worlds; "Bharga" because he colors (*rañjayati*) these beings; "Gacchati" (he goes) because these creatures go toward him and come from him; therefore, because of his burning (*bhāraka*), he is Bharga. Because he is born forth (*sūyamāna*) as the enemy, he is Sūrya; because of his impelling (*savana*), he is Savitṛ; because of his giving (*dāna*), he is Āditya; because of his purifying (*pavana*), he is Pāvamāna. Furthermore, "Āya" (he comes) and "Āyanāt" (because of his coming), thus he is Āditya; for thus it is said.

Indeed, the self, called the immortal, is the knower, the thinker, the goer, the creator, the delighter, the agent, the speaker, the taster, the smeller, and the toucher; it is the pervasive one established within the body—thus indeed they say. Now, where consciousness has become dualistic, there one hears, sees, smells, tastes, touches, and the self knows all. But where consciousness has become non-dualistic, free from cause and effect, beyond description, incomparable, and indefinable—how, my dear, can that be expressed in words?

7. For this indeed is the Self, the Lord, Śambhu, Bhava, Rudra, Prajāpati, the Creator of the Universe, Hiraṇyagarbha, Truth, Prāṇa, Haṃsa, the Peaceful, Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Arka, Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, Samrāj, Indra, and Indu. He who shines there, veiled by fire, by the thousand-eyed golden one, and by bliss—this very one is indeed to be sought to be known. Having granted freedom from fear to all beings, having gone to the forest, then...

One perceives him as having cast out the objects of the senses from one's own body; he is the one of universal form, the golden-hued, the knower of all births, the supreme goal, the sole light that shines intensely. This sun, the breath of all creatures, rises with a thousand rays, manifesting itself in a hundred ways. (5.8) Thus ends the fifth chapter.

Now begins the sixth chapter. This Prāṇa indeed sustains itself in two ways: that which is this [breath] and that which is yonder Āditya (the sun). Furthermore, these two paths of his are internal and external; by means of day and night, these two revolve. Yonder Āditya is the outer self (*bahirātmā*), and the Prāṇa is the inner self (*antarātmā*). Therefore, by the movement of the outer self, the movement of the inner self is inferred. For thus it is said: "Now, whoever is a knower, free from evil, the overseer of the senses, pure-minded, established in That, with eyes turned inward—he [perceives] by means of the movement of the inner self."

"The movement of the inner self is inferred from that which is outside"—thus it was said. Now, that golden person who is within the sun, who looks down upon this golden earth—he, indeed, is seated within the lotus of the heart and eats food.

Now, he who dwells within the lotus of the heart and eats food—he is that very fire, the solar one situated in heaven, called Time, invisible, who eats all beings as his food. What is this lotus, and of what is it composed? This lotus is indeed this space (ākāśa); its four quarters and four intermediate directions are the arrangement of its petals. These two—the vital breath (prāṇa) and the sun—move about within it from all sides. One should worship these by means of the syllable "Om," the Vyāhṛtis, and the Sāvitrī verse. || 2 ||

There are indeed two forms of Brahman: the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*). Now, that which is formed is the unreal; that which is formless is the real, that is Brahman, that is the Light. That which is the Light is the Āditya. This very one became the self (*ātman*) as the syllable *om*. He divided himself threefold—*om*, thus [he did]. These are the three morae (*mātrā*); by these, "I am woven across and through all this," he thought. For thus it has been said: "One should meditate upon the Āditya as *om* and thus yoke the self. 3.
Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere: "Now, that which is the Udgītha is the Praṇava; that which is the Praṇava is the Udgītha. Indeed, yonder sun is the Udgītha; he is the Praṇava."

For thus it is said: "One should know the Udgītha, called Praṇava, the leader, whose form is light, free from sleep, free from old age, free from death, having three feet and three syllables, which is again fivefold and hidden in the cave. And thus it is said: "The Brahman with its root above and three feet; the branches are space, air, fire, water, earth, and so forth. This one is named Aśvattha; this is that Brahman. Its splendor is this sun. And this belongs to the syllable 'Om'; therefore, one should worship this by means of 'Om' incessantly"—this is one [aspect] of it.
Thus, in order to instruct [the disciple], he said: "This very syllable is meritorious; this very syllable is supreme. Having known this very syllable, whatever one desires, that shall be his. (4)

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "This body of his is resonant with the syllable *om*; it possesses gender as female, male, and neuter; it is radiant as fire, wind, and the sun; it possesses sovereignty as Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu; it possesses mouths as the Gārhapatya, Dakṣiṇāgni, and Āhavanīya fires; it possesses consciousness as the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman; it possesses worlds as Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar; it possesses time as the past, present, and future; and it possesses life-force as Prāṇa, Agni, and Sūrya."

"This [Om] is possessed of majesty, for it attains food, water, and the moon; it is possessed of nourishment, for it causes growth; it is possessed of consciousness, for it comprises intellect, mind, and ego; it is possessed of vital breath, for it comprises prāṇa, apāna, and vyāna. Thus, when 'Om' is uttered, these [powers] are introduced, honored, and established. For thus it has been said: "O Satyakāma, this syllable 'Om' is indeed both the higher and the lower Brahman. || 5 ||

Now, this [universe] was indeed unuttered. That Prajāpati, who is Truth, having performed austerity, uttered it forth: "Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svar. This is the most substantial body of that Prajāpati, namely that which possesses the worlds. Of this [body], "Svar" is the head, "Bhuvaḥ" is the navel, and "Bhūḥ" is the feet; the sun is the eye. For the eye is the great measure of a person, since by means of the eye a person traverses the great measure. Indeed, the eye is truth, for established in the eye, a person moves among all objects.

Therefore, one should meditate upon it as "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. For by this, Prajāpati, the self of all and the eye of all, becomes meditated upon. Thus it is said: "This indeed is the all-sustaining body of Prajāpati; in it all this is contained, and in all this that [body] is contained. Therefore, one should meditate upon it. || 6 ||

Regarding the verse, "Tat savitur vareṇyam" (That excellent glory of Savitṛ): the Brahman-knowers say that Savitṛ is indeed the Sun, and he is to be chosen by one who desires the Self. Then, regarding "Bhargo devasya dhīmahi" (We meditate upon the glory of the God): the Brahman-knowers say that Savitṛ is indeed the God, and therefore we contemplate that which is called his "glory. Then, regarding "Dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt" (Who may impel our thoughts): the Brahman-knowers say that "thoughts" (*dhiyaḥ*) are indeed the intellects (*buddhayaḥ*), and [the phrase means] "may He impel those of us. Now, regarding "Bharga": it is that which is placed in yonder Sun, and that which is in the eye.

This is indeed Bharga; for his movement is by means of light (*bhābhiḥ*), thus he is Bharga; or because he burns (*bharjayati*), he is Bharga—thus say the exponents of Brahman. Furthermore, *bha* because he illumines these worlds; *ra* because he delights these beings; *ga* because these creatures go (*gacchanti*) unto him and come (*āgacchanti*) from him. Therefore, because of his being the refuge (*bhara-gatvāt*), he is Bharga. Because he is eternally being born (*śāśvat sūyamānāt*), he is Sūrya; because of his impelling (*savanāt*), he is Savitṛ; because of his taking up (*ādānāt*), he is Āditya; because of his purifying (*pavanāt*), he is Pāvana. And because he nourishes (*āpyāyanāt*), he is Apaḥ. For thus it is said: "He is truly the Self of the Self."

The pervasive Lord is established within the body as the one who leads, the one called immortal, the knower, the thinker, the goer, the one who has cast off [suffering], the one who causes bliss, the agent, the speaker, the taster, the smeller, the seer, the hearer, and the toucher. For thus it is said: "Now, where cognition has become dualistic, there indeed one hears, sees, smells, tastes, touches, and the Self knows everything. But where cognition has become non-dualistic—freed from cause, effect, and action, beyond description, incomparable, and indefinable—what can that be called?"

7. For he indeed is the Self, the Lord, Śambhu, Bhava, Rudra, Prajāpati, the Creator of the universe, Hiraṇyagarbha, Truth, Prāṇa, Haṃsa, the Teacher, Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Arka, Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Samrāj, Indra, and Indu—he who shines like fire, yet is veiled by fire within a golden egg with a thousand eyes. Verily, this is what one should desire to know and seek after; having granted safety to all beings, one should go to the forest and then [seek him].

Having cast aside the objects of the senses from his own body, one should perceive him thus: "The omniform, golden Jātavedas, the ultimate resort, the single light that shines; with a thousand rays, existing in a hundred ways, this Sun rises as the life-breath of all creatures. || 8 ||

Therefore, this knower of the two-fold nature meditates upon the Self alone and sacrifices to the Self alone; thus meditation is praised by the wise as the mind established in the performance [of sacrifice]. One should purify that mind with the verse: "The mind defiled by impurity, by leavings, and by what is struck by evil"—with this he recites the mantra: "That which is defiled by leavings, that which is given by a sinner, or from one who is in a state of death-impurity or birth-impurity—may the purifier of Vasu, Agni, and the rays of Savitṛ purify my food and whatever other evil there may be. With water he first surrounds it for the sake of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

He offers oblations with five [mantras]: "Svāhā to the out-breath! Svāhā to the diffused breath! Svāhā to the equalizing breath! Svāhā to the up-breath! Svāhā! Then, restraining his speech, he eats what remains. Thereafter, he again covers [the food] from above with water. Having sipped water and become purified, he should meditate upon himself with two mantras: "The breath is Agni; you are the All" and "The breath is Agni, the Supreme Self; indeed, the fivefold wind has taken refuge in you. May he, being pleased, please the All; you are the consumer of the All, the All; you are Vaiśvānara; by you the All is sustained."
"May all oblations enter you as you are being born; may all creatures be where you are, O Immortal One. By this very rite, one indeed returns again to the state of being the eater. || 9 ||

Now, furthermore, another subsequent modification of this sacrifice to the Self (ātmayajña) should be understood, namely: "the food and the eater of food. Its detailed explanation is as follows: the conscious person (puruṣa), situated within the Pradhāna, is the enjoyer who consumes the food derived from Prakṛti. Of that [enjoyer], this elemental self (bhūtātman) is indeed the food, while the Pradhāna is its maker. Therefore, the three qualities (guṇas) are the object of enjoyment, and the person situated within is the enjoyer. In this regard, there is the empirical evidence known as "perception," because since animals originate from seeds, the seed is thus the food of the Pradhāna.

The state of being "edible" has been explained; therefore, the Puruṣa is the enjoyer and Prakṛti is the object of enjoyment. Abiding therein, he enjoys the food of Prakṛti, which—because it transforms through the differentiation of the three guṇas—consists of the principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas, as well as the subtle body (liṅga). By this very [explanation], the exposition of the fourteen-fold path is accomplished. For this world, having become food, is characterized by pleasure, pain, and delusion. Indeed, there is no grasping of sweetness in a seed until its production [as a plant]; likewise, even for that [seed], the state of being food exists in three stages, beginning with childhood.

Just as youth transforms into old age, so too does that very [substance] reach the state of manifestation (vyaktatā) for the primary cause (pradhāna). In that state, the intellect and the other faculties become "delicious food" (svādūni), consisting of determination (adhyavasāya), volition (saṅkalpa), and self-conceit (abhimāna). Then, the objects of the senses become "delicious food" within the five [senses]. Thus, all the functions of the senses and the functions of the vital breaths (prāṇa) are likewise [food]. Manifest matter (vyakta) is the food, and unmanifest matter (avyakta) is the food; its enjoyer is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), and from the fact of being an enjoyer, consciousness (caitanya) is established for it. Just as Agni is indeed the eater of food among the gods.

"Soma is food; by fire alone is food [consumed]. One who knows thus—that this self, known as Soma, is also known as Agni because of the statement "with the unmanifest as its mouth"—is indeed a person who, through the unmanifest as his mouth, enjoys the three qualities (guṇas). He who knows this is a renunciant (saṃnyāsī), a yogi, and a self-sacrificer (ātmayājī). Furthermore, just as one does not touch women who have entered an empty house, so too he who does not touch the objects of the senses even when they have entered [the senses] is a renunciant, a yogi, and a self-sacrificer. || 10 ||

Food, indeed, is the supreme form of the self, for this vital breath (*prāṇa*) consists of food. Now, if one does not eat, one becomes a non-thinker, a non-hearer, a non-toucher, a non-seer, a non-speaker, a non-smeller, and a non-taster, and one gives up the vital breaths. Thus it is said: "But if, indeed, one eats, having become enriched by the vital breath, one becomes a thinker, a hearer, a toucher, a speaker, a taster, a smeller, and a seer. Thus it is said: "From food, indeed, creatures are born."

Some depend on the earth; therefore they live by food alone, and in the end they even pass away into it. Moreover, it is said elsewhere: "Indeed, all these beings fall day after day into food, desiring to seize it. The sun takes up food with its rays, and by that he shines. These vital breaths cook [digest] when sprinkled with food; indeed, fire blazes because of food. This world was fashioned by Brahmā out of a desire for food. Therefore, one should meditate upon food as the Self," for so it says.

"Non-existent things are born; once born, they grow by means of food. It is eaten and it eats beings; therefore, it is called 'food' (anna). Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "This body which is food is indeed the 'All-Sustainer' (viśvabhṛt), the form of the blessed Viṣṇu. Breath is the essence of food; mind is the essence of breath; consciousness is the essence of mind; and bliss is the essence of consciousness. He who knows this becomes possessed of food, possessed of breath, possessed of mind, possessed of consciousness, and possessed of bliss—just as far as these [qualities] extend here.

Beings eat food only so long as one who knows this eats the food residing within himself. Food indeed is the conqueror of old age; food is remembered as the means of reconciliation. Food is the life-breath of animals; food is the eldest; food is remembered as the physician. (13)

Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere: "Food is the source of this entire universe, and time is the source of food; the sun is the source of time. Its form is that which is composed from the units of time beginning with the *nimeṣa* [the twinkle of an eye], namely the year consisting of twelve parts. Half of this is fiery (*āgneya*) and half is watery (*vāruṇa*). The half beginning with Maghā up to the middle of Śraviṣṭhā is fiery; in forward and reverse order, the half beginning with Āśleṣā up to the end of the middle of Śraviṣṣṭhā is lunar (*saumya*). In each of these, there is one ninth part of the self, which is of various kinds according to its movement; because of its subtlety, this is the measure by means of this very [year]."

For time is measured; indeed, there is no perception of an object of knowledge (*prameya*) without a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Even the object of knowledge attains the state of being a means of knowledge through its distinctness, for the purpose of self-awakening. Thus it is said: "As many as are the parts of time, so many [parts] does he traverse who meditates on time as Brahman; time recedes far away from him. Thus it is also said: "From time beings flow forth; by time they attain growth; in time they set; time is both the formed and the formless. (14)

There are indeed two forms of Brahman: Time and Non-Time. Now, that which is prior to the sun is Non-Time; it is formless. But that which begins with the sun is Time; it is possessed of form. This year is indeed the form of that which possesses form. From the year, verily, these creatures are born; by the year they grow once born; in the year they pass away. Therefore, the year is Prajāpati, Time, Food, and the Abode of Brahman, and the Self. Thus it is said: "Time ripens all beings."

All these indeed reside within the Great Self. He in whom time is cooked—he who knows him is a knower of the Veda. This Time is embodied; he is the King of the Ocean of Creatures, residing therein as the one called Savitṛ, from whom these—the moon, the stars, the planets, the years, and so forth—are produced. From them, whatever exists here in this world, whether auspicious or inauspicious, is seen to arise. Therefore, one should worship the Sun, whose essence is Brahmā, under the name of Time. Some say that the Sun is Brahmā. Thus [ends the section].
For thus it is said: "The sacrificer, the enjoyer, the oblation, the mantra, the sacrifice, Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, the All, Someone, the Lord, and the Witness—he who shines in that orb. (16)

In the beginning, indeed, this was Brahman alone—endless in the east, endless in the south, endless in the west, endless in the north, endless above and below, and endless in every direction. For in its case, the directions such as the east do not exist; nor do the intermediate directions, nor the upward or downward directions. This Supreme Self is beyond the reach of logic, inconceivable, and immeasurable. He is the space-self (*ākāśātman*); he alone is the one who remains awake when all else has perished. From this space, he indeed awakens this mere consciousness, and by him alone is this world meditated upon.

And when this [body] perishes, that radiant form of his—which is the light that shines in yonder sun, and the light in smokeless fire, and the most wonderful light within the belly that digests food—is likewise withdrawn. For thus it is said: "That which is in the fire, that which is in the heart, and that which is in the sun—that is this one alone. Indeed, he who knows this attains oneness with the One. 17.

Likewise, the practice of that [yoga] consists of six limbs: breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), meditation (dhyāna), concentration (dhāraṇā), deliberation (tarka), and absorption (samādhi); this is called yoga. When, by means of this, the seer beholds the golden-hued creator, the Lord, the Puruṣa who is the source of Brahman, then the knower, having abandoned merit and sin, unifies everything in the supreme, imperishable state. Thus it is said: "Just as deer and birds do not take refuge on a mountain ablaze with fire, even so faults never take refuge in the knower of Brahman. (18)

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "When indeed the wise man, having restrained the mind externally and having caused the senses to enter into the objects of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), should then remain free from conceptual construction (*niḥsaṅkalpa*); because here the living being known as *prāṇa* has arisen from that which is beyond *prāṇa*, therefore one should indeed sustain the *prāṇa* within that which is called the Fourth (*turya*)—for thus he says: 'The thoughtless thought situated in the midst of thought, inconceivable, secret, and supreme; there the mind should be placed, and that sign (*liṅga*) is without support. (19)

Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere: "Therefore, his supreme concentration (*dhāraṇā*) arises from pressing the palate and the tip of the tongue, and from the restraint of speech, mind, and breath. Through inquiry, he perceives Brahman; when, through the self, he perceives the Self—smaller than the smallest, shining—he sees the Self by means of the self through the dissolution of the mind. Having seen the Self by means of the self, he becomes selfless (*nirātmā*). Because of being selfless, he is the immeasurable, the unborn, the inconceivable—the characteristic of liberation. This is the supreme secret. Thus it is said: "Indeed, by the tranquility of the mind, one destroys both auspicious and inauspicious karma."

"Having become serene in soul and abiding in the Self, one attains imperishable bliss. (20) Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "The upward-tending channel called *suṣumnā* is the path for the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). It is severed within the palate. Through that [channel], joined with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), the mind, and the vital breath, one should ascend upwards. Having turned back the tip of the palate and not engaging the senses, the Great One should behold the Greatness. Thereafter, one goes beyond the state of having a self; because of being selfless, one does not partake in pleasure or pain, and attains isolation (*kaivalya*). For thus he says:

Having first established the supreme [state] and then restrained the breath, one who has crossed to the further shore by means of that which is shoreless should subsequently apply himself to the upward path. Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "There are indeed two Brahmans to be meditated upon: the Word and the Non-Word. Now, by the Word alone is the Non-Word revealed. Then, therein, the sound 'Om'—having ascended upwards by means of this—attains its dissolution in the Non-Word. This, they say, is the goal; this is the immortal; this is union with That (tatsāyujyatva); this is liberation. And so it is. And then:

Just as a spider, having ascended by means of its thread, finds open space, even so indeed does this meditator, having ascended by means of the syllable *Oṃ*, attain independence. Otherwise, there are others who maintain the doctrine of sound (*śabdavādinaḥ*): through the union of the ear and the thumb, they hear the sound of the ether within the heart. This has seven varieties; its analogies are as follows: a river, a small bell, bronze, a wheel, a frog, a bird, and a cricket; it speaks like rain in a windless place. Having transcended that which possesses these distinct characteristics—

When they have set in the supreme, unmanifest Brahman, they become non-distinct in their attributes and non-distinct in their discernibility, just as various juices that have attained the state of honey [become indistinguishable]. Thus it is said: "Two Brahmans are to be known—the Brahman of Sound (Śabdabrahman) and that which is the Supreme (Parā). One who is proficient in the Brahman of Sound attains the Supreme Brahman. (22)

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "That which is sound is this syllable *oṃ*. That which is its tip is the peaceful, beyond sound, fearless, sorrowless, blissful, satisfied, steady, immovable, immortal, infallible, and eternal, designated as Viṣṇu; for the sake of attaining the state beyond all else, one should worship that. Thus he says: 'This deity, who is both supreme and non-supreme, is by name called *Oṃkāra*; being soundless and having become void, one should practice [meditation] upon him in the place of the crown of the head. (23)

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "The body is the bow, 'Om' is the arrow; its tip is the mind. Having pierced through the darkness characterized by ignorance, one reaches that which is beyond darkness. Then, having pierced through that which is enveloped [by light], one beholds Brahman—shining like a whirling firebrand, radiant as the sun, full of splendor, beyond all darkness—that which shines in yonder sun, in the moon, in the fire, and in lightning. Indeed, having seen this, one attains immortality. Thus it is said: "Meditation is directed inward toward the supreme reality and toward the objects of focus."

It is deposited; therefore, undifferentiated consciousness attains differentiation. When the mental faculty has dissolved, that bliss which is witnessed by the Self—that is Brahman, the immortal, the pure; that is the goal, and that indeed is the world. || 24 ||

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "He who, with his senses withdrawn in sleep, sees as if in a dream within the cavity of the senses by means of an intellect consisting of purest clarity—himself free from constraint—the Guide known as *praṇava*, whose form is light, and who is free from sleep, free from old age, free from death, and free from sorrow; he too becomes known as *praṇava*, the Guide, whose form is light, and is free from sleep, free from old age, free from death, and free from sorrow. For thus it is said: "In this way, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the syllable *oṃ* [are one], because everything is manifoldly [derived] from that."

Because one joins (*yunakti*) or is joined (*yuñjate*), it is traditionally known as *yoga*. The unification of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the mind (*manas*), and likewise the senses, as well as the renunciation of all states of being, is designated as *yoga*. || 25 ||

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "Just as a fowler, having caught water-birds with a stringed trap, offers them into the fire in his belly, even so, indeed, he draws out these vital breaths (prāṇas) by means of this 'Om' and offers them into the fire of the Self (anāmaye 'gnau). Therefore, from that heated earth, just as clarified butter on heated earth blazes up upon contact with grass and wood, even so, indeed, this [fire] called the Non-breath (aprāṇa) blazes up through contact with the vital breaths. Now, that which blazes is the form of Brahman, and this is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu."

This is the Rudra-nature of Rudra; having divided himself in immeasurable ways, he thus fills these worlds. For it is said: "Just as sparks indeed issue from fire, and likewise rays from the sun, so too do the vital breaths (prāṇas) and the rest emerge from him here in due order. || 26 ||

Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere: "This heat of the body belongs to Brahman—the supreme, immortal, bodiless one; this [heat] is its clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Now, being manifest, it is deposited in the sky. Indeed, with one-pointedness, they thus pierce the space within the heart, whereby it becomes like a light. Therefore, it attains that state before long, just as an iron mass placed on the ground quickly attains the nature of the earth. Just as blacksmiths and others do not overcome an iron mass when it is in the form of clay."

The mind perishes together with its substratum in this very manner; for thus it is said: "The sheath consisting of the space within the heart is bliss, the supreme abode; from that comes our own yoga, as well as the splendor of both fire and the sun. (27)

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "Having transcended the elements, the senses, and their objects, one takes up the bow whose string is fortitude and whose staff is self-control; then, with an arrow consisting of non-conceit, one slays that first gatekeeper, Brahmā, who has delusion for his crown, thirst for his earrings, sloth for his bowstring, pride for his chief minister, and anger for his bowstring. Taking up the bow whose staff is greed and whose string is desire, one slays these very beings with an arrow consisting of longing. Having slain him, one crosses to the further shore of the space within the heart by means of the raft of the syllable *Oṃ*."

Having crossed over, when the intermediate space has appeared, he who desires the elements enters the pit slowly, as if into a natural hollow; in this manner, he should enter the hall of Brahman (*brahmaśālā*). Then, by means of the Guru’s instruction, he should push open the four-layered treasury of Brahman (*brahmakośa*). Thus, being pure, purified, void, tranquil, breathless, selfless, infinite, imperishable, stable, eternal, unborn, and independent, he abides in his own majesty. Having seen him abiding in his own majesty, one perceives the wheel of movement as if it were a wheel that no longer revolves. Thus indeed it is said:

But for the embodied one who is disciplined for six months and is constantly liberated, the supreme and most secret perfect yoga proceeds; yet it never occurs for the embodied one who is pierced by passion and darkness, who is intensely inflamed [by worldly desires], and who is attached to children, wife, and family.

Having spoken thus, Śākāyanya vanished within his heart. Having paid homage to him, [the king reflected: "O King, by means of this knowledge of Brahman, the sons of Prajāpati have ascended the path of Brahman. Through the practice of yoga, one attains contentment, endurance of the pairs of opposites, and tranquility. This most secret [teaching] should not be proclaimed to one who is not a son, nor to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who is not tranquil; it should be given to one who is devoted to none other and endowed with all virtues. || 29 ||

"Oṃ! In a pure place, being pure himself, established in goodness (*sattva*), studying the truth, speaking the truth, meditating on the truth, and performing sacrifice to the truth—one should become such. Therefore, through cessation from activity directed toward the True Brahman which desires the Truth, one whose bonds are severed by that fruit becomes free from desire; regarding others as oneself, being devoid of fear, and free from longing, one stands having ascended to imperishable and immeasurable bliss. Indeed, the supreme extraction of the highest treasure is this very state of desirelessness.

For that person, consisting of all desires and characterized by determination, volition, and egoism, is bound; therefore, one who is the opposite of that is liberated. Regarding this, some say: "The quality (guṇa), under the influence of the differentiation of primordial nature (prakṛti), has entered into bondage through the self-nature of determination."

Liberation indeed comes from the destruction of the defects of mental determination (*adhyavasāya*). For one sees with the mind alone, and with the mind one hears. Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear—all this is the mind alone. When carried away by the flood of the *guṇas* and rendered turbid, it becomes unstable, fickle, distracted, full of longing, and agitated; thus having fallen into the state of egoism, thinking "I am that" and "this is mine," it binds itself by itself, like a bird caught in its own web.

Therefore, the person (puruṣa) is bound when characterized by determination, volition, and egoism; conversely, he is liberated when the opposite is true. Consequently, one should remain free from determination, free from volition, and free from egoism—this is the mark of liberation. This is the path to Brahman here; this is the opening of the door here, through which one will go to the further shore of this darkness. For it is said: "When the five [senses] of knowledge stand still together with the mind..."

"When the intellect no longer functions, they call that the supreme goal. Having said this, Śākāyanya vanished; having paid his respects to him and performed the proper rites, Marut, having accomplished his purpose, departed for the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), for there is no return from there. This is the path to Brahman here: "Having pierced the solar door, they have gone forth upwards"—regarding this they cite: "Infinite are its rays, like a lamp situated in the heart—white, black, tawny, blue, brown, and pale red."

One ray of these stands above; having pierced the solar orb and transcended the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka), by it they go to the supreme goal. Another hundred rays of his which are situated upwards, by them he attains the abodes of the hosts of gods. Those many-colored rays of his below which possess gentle luster—by means of them, he transmigrates downward for the experience of karma in this world. Therefore, this blessed Āditya is the cause of creation, heaven, and liberation. || 30 ||

"What is the nature of these senses as they function? Who here is their originator and controller? To this he says: "They have the Self (ātman) as their essence. For the Self is indeed their originator. Now, there are the Apsarases and the rays called Bhānavīyas; with five of these rays, it consumes the objects of the senses. "Which one is the Self? It is that which has been described by characteristics such as being pure, stainless, empty, and tranquil, and which is to be grasped by its own signs. This is the sign of that signless one: namely, the heat manifested in fire, and that which is the most auspicious essence of the waters.

Thus say some. Then others say: speech, hearing, sight, mind, and breath; or else, intellect, fortitude, memory, and wisdom—that is it. Now, these [emanate] from this very one, just as here on earth sprouts emerge from a seed, or as smoke, flame, and sparks from fire. Regarding this, they cite the following: "Just as sparks indeed from fire, and likewise rays from the sun, so too do the vital breaths and the rest emerge from that one here in due order. (31)

From this very Self, indeed, all vital breaths, all worlds, all Vedas, all deities, and all beings emerge. Its secret name (*upaniṣad*) is "the Truth of truth. Now, just as various clouds of smoke issue forth from a fire when damp fuel is added, even so, this Rigveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, Atharvāṅgirasa, history, ancient lore, sciences, secret names, verses, aphorisms, explanations, and commentaries are the breath of this great Being.

All these beings are indeed its explanations. This Agni, the year, consists of five bricks; these are his bricks: spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, and winter. He is head, wings, back, and tail; this Agni knows the person. This is the first layer of Prajāpati. Having lifted the sacrificer up to the intermediate space with his hands, he delivered him to Vāyu. Vāyu is indeed breath; Agni is breath. These are his bricks: inhalation (*prāṇa*), exhalation (*vyāna*), downward breath (*apāna*), diffused breath (*samāna*), and upward breath (*udāna*).

Having a head, wings, a back, and a tail, this Agni is man-shaped; that is this intermediate space, the second layer of Prajāpati. With his hands, he lifted the sacrificer up to heaven and delivered him to Indra. That sun, indeed, is Indra; he is this Agni. Its bricks are the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, Atharvāṅgirasa, Itihāsa, and Purāṇa. Having a head, wings, a tail, and a back, this Agni is man-shaped; that is this sky, the third layer of Prajāpati.

With his hands, he makes an offering for the sacrificer to the Knower of the Self, just as the Knower of the Self, having lifted it up, presented it to Brahman; therein he becomes blissful and joyful. The earth is the Gārhapatya fire, the intermediate space is the Dakṣiṇāgni, and the sky is the Āhavanīya. From these very [fires] come Pavamāna, Pāvaka, and Śuci. By this, his sacrifice is made manifest, because the digestive fire (jāṭhara) is indeed a collection of Pavamāna, Pāvaka, and Śuci. Therefore, Agni is to be sacrificed to, to be kindled, to be praised, and to be meditated upon. Having taken the oblation, the sacrificer—

He desires meditation upon the deity; he also investigates the meaning of the mantra: "The golden-colored bird, established in the heart and in the sun—the Madgu, the swan, the bull of splendor—him we worship in this fire."

The most excellent splendor of that Savitṛ is to be meditated upon; he who, dwelling within the intellect as a meditator, pursues here the state of peace of the mind, places it in the Self alone. On this subject, there are these verses: 1. Just as a fire without fuel is extinguished in its own source, so the mind, through the cessation of its fluctuations, is extinguished in its own source. 2. For the mind that has been extinguished in its own source and is free from desire for reality, the objects of the senses—though they follow the power of karma—are unreal to one who is deluded regarding them.

3. The mind alone is indeed saṃsāra; one should purify it with diligent effort. For whatever the mind is intent upon, that one becomes; this is an eternal secret. 4. Indeed, by the tranquility of the mind, one destroys both auspicious and inauspicious karma. With a tranquil self, abiding in the Self, one enjoys imperishable bliss. 5. Just as the mind of a living being is intensely attached to the sphere of sense-objects, if it were likewise so toward Brahman, who would not be liberated from bondage?

6. The mind is indeed said to be of two kinds: pure and impure. It is impure through contact with desire, and pure when devoid of desire. 7. Having made the mind perfectly steady, free from both dissolution and distraction, when it reaches the state of non-mind, that is the supreme state. 8. The mind should be restrained within the heart until it reaches its dissolution; this is both knowledge and liberation, while all else are merely extensive elaborations of books.

9. The bliss that arises when the mind, cleansed of impurities by *samādhi*, is established in the Self, cannot be described by speech; at that time, it is apprehended by the inner organ itself. 10. Just as water does not perceive water, nor fire in fire, nor space in space, so he whose mind has entered within is completely liberated. 11. The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings; attached to sense objects, it leads to bondage; free from sense objects, it is known as liberation.

Therefore, for those who do not maintain the *agnihotra* fire, who have not built the sacrificial fire-altar (*agni-cit*), and who do not possess knowledge or meditative contemplation, the recollection of the Brahman’s station in the void is impossible. Consequently, the fire must be maintained, built, praised, and meditated upon. 34.

Homage to Agni, who dwells on earth, who remembers the world; grant a world to this sacrificer! Homage to Vāyu, who dwells in the intermediate space, who remembers the world; grant a world to this sacrificer! Homage to Āditya, who dwells in heaven, who remembers the world; grant a world to this sacrificer! Homage to Brahmā, who dwells in all, who remembers all; grant everything to this sacrificer! The face of truth is covered by a golden vessel. O Pūṣan, uncover it for Viṣṇu, whose nature is truth, for him who is that [Brahman].

The person in the sun—that is indeed I. This is truly the Satya-dharma (the Law of Truth), which is the solar nature of the sun. That white, signless person within the sky is merely a portion of the light that has entered the atmosphere; this is what is in the center of the sun, as it were. This is in the eye and in the fire. This is Brahman; this is the Immortal; this is Bharga. This is Satya-dharma; it is merely a portion of the light that has entered the atmosphere. This is the Immortal in the center of the sun, of which Soma is the sprout and the vital breaths are the roots.

This is Brahman; this is the Immortal; this is Bharga. This is the True Dharma, a mere fraction of the splendor contained within the ether. It is that which shines as the Yajus-mantra in the midst of the sun—the Umā, the waters, the light, the essence, the immortal, the Brahman, Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ Om.

The pure swan with eight feet, consisting of three threads, subtle and imperishable, blind to duality yet kindled by splendor—he who sees all sees this: that which is but a minute portion of the light situated within the sky, which, having risen in the midst of the sun, becomes two rays; this is Savitṛ, this is the True Dharma, this is the Yajus, this is austerity, this is Agni, this is Vāyu, this is Prāṇa, this is Water, this is the Moon, this is the Bright, this is the Immortal, this is the realm of Brahman, this is the Light-Ocean; in that very ocean is the sacrificer, like a lump of salt.

They seem to dissolve away; this indeed is the oneness with Brahman, for here all desires are contained. Regarding this they cite: "Like a stream of particles driven by a subtle wind, that which is within the gods flashes forth. He who knows thus is a knower of the Sun, a knower of duality, and one who has attained the single light; he becomes of that very nature. Those which rise up incessantly like drops, or like the flashes of lightning in the highest heaven—these are indeed the rays of glory, appearing as if with matted locks because of their dwelling in the abode of fame, like the flames of the black-pathed fire (Agni). || 35 ||

Indeed, these two are the forms of the Brahman-light: one is the tranquil and the other is the prosperous. Now, that which is tranquil has space as its support; and that which is prosperous has this [world] as its food. Therefore, one should sacrifice upon the sacrificial ground with mantras, herbs, clarified butter, meat, sacrificial cakes, cooked offerings in pots, and so forth; and with the remnants of food and drink remaining on the *āvasathya* fire, one should offer them into the *āhavanīya* fire, thinking thus for the prosperity of one's vital energy, for the sake of conquering the worlds of merit, and for the attainment of immortality. Regarding this, they cite: "One who desires heaven should perform the *agnihotra*."

One attains the realm of Yama by means of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, the realm of Soma by the Uktha, the realm of Sūrya by the Ṣoḍaśin, self-sovereignty (svārājya) by the Atirātra, and the realm of Prajāpati by the sacrifice that culminates in a thousand years. Just as the stability of a lamp depends on the wick, the fuel, and the oil, so too do these two worlds depend upon the internal cosmic egg for their existence within the Self. || 36 ||

Therefore, one should worship this immeasurable splendor with the syllable *om*. It is declared to be threefold: in fire, in the sun, and in the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Now, this channel called "abundance of food" carries what is offered into the fire toward the sun; from that, the essence which flowed down rains as the *udgītha*. By that, these vital breaths exist, and from the vital breaths, living beings arise. Regarding this, they cite: "The oblation that is poured into the fire, that it causes to go to the sun; the sun rains by means of its rays; thereby food comes into being; from food arises the birth of all beings. For thus it is said in the *Agni-vidyā*: "In the fire..."

The oblation properly offered reaches the sun; from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings. (37) One who offers the *agnihotra* oblation pierces the net of greed; then, having cut through delusion, praising no more through anger and contemplating desire no longer, he pierces the four-layered sheath of Brahman. From there, having pierced the spheres of the sun, the moon, and fire—which belong to the quality of goodness—he reaches the supreme ether. There, purified, he attains the immovable, immortal, and infallible state situated within the essence of pure being.

One beholds that which is certainly designated as Viṣṇu, the supreme abode of all, endowed with true desire and omniscience, independent consciousness abiding in its own glory. Regarding this, they cite: "The Moon is situated in the midst of the Sun; in the midst of the Moon is the Fire; in the midst of the Radiance is the Essence (Sattva); and in the midst of the Essence abides the Imperishable (Acyuta)."

Having meditated on the connection of the body, the span of a thumb, and the atom, one thereafter attains the state beyond this; for here all desires are contained. Regarding this, they cite: "The Great God, whose body is the measure of a thumb and a span, has entered the worlds in three ways like the heat of a lamp's flame—that Brahman which is praised. Om! Salutations to Brahman! Salutations! Thus ends the sixth chapter.

Prapāṭhaka 7. Agni, the Gāyatra, the Trivṛt, the Rathantara, the spring, the vital breath, the stars, and the Vasus rise in the east; they heat, they rain, they praise, and they withdraw again. They look within the midst of the void. He is inconceivable, formless, profound, the enjoyer of qualities, beyond rebirth, the Lord of Yoga, omniscient, bountiful, immeasurable, without beginning or end, glorious, unborn, wise, indefinable, the creator of all, the Self of all, the consumer of all, the ruler of all, and the innermost within all. 1.

Indra, the Triṣṭubh meter, the Pañcadaśa-stoma, the Bṛhat-sāman, the summer season, the Vyāna-vital breath, Soma, and the Rudras rise from the south; they heat, rain, praise, and again enter [the world]. They look through the internal aperture—he who is without beginning or end, immeasurable, undivided, not dependent on another, independent, signless, formless, possessed of infinite power, the Ordainer, the Maker of Light. || 2 ||

The Maruts, the Jagatī meter, the seventeenfold Stoma, the Vairūpa Sāman, the rainy season, and the Apāna breath—these are the Śukra Ādityas. Rising from behind, they heat, rain, praise, and again enter [the world]. In the beginning, Prajāpati alone existed; he did not find delight being alone. He meditated upon himself and created many offspring. He beheld them as if they were lifeless, standing like pillars, awakened from his own self. He did not find delight in that. He thought, "I shall enter within these to awaken them. Then, having made himself like the wind, he entered within. Being one, he did not enter; dividing himself fivefold, he is called Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, Udāna, and Vyāna.

Now, that which moves upward is indeed the *prāṇa*; that which moves downward is indeed the *apāna*; that which establishes the coarsest food-essence in the *apāna* and evenly distributes the subtlest [essence] to every limb is indeed the *samāna*; that which ejects and swallows what has been drunk and eaten is indeed the *udāna*; and that by which these channels are pervaded is indeed the *vyāna*. || 2.7 ||

Then the Upāṃśu cup overcomes the Antaryāma cup, and the Antaryāma cup overcomes the Upāṃśu cup; in the interval between these two is heat, a fleshy lump of heat—that is the person (puruṣa). Now, that which is the person is Agni Vaiśvānara. It has also been stated elsewhere: "This is Agni Vaiśvānara, who is this infinite person by whom this food is cooked—namely, that which is eaten. His sound is heard when one covers his ears and listens. When he is about to depart [from the body], he no longer hears that sound. || 2.8 ||

This very Self, having divided itself fivefold, is placed within the cave [of the heart], consisting of mind, having vital breath for its body, possessing many forms, and characterized by true resolve. This very Self, dwelling within his heart, thinking "I have not accomplished my purpose; let me attain my goals," pierced these openings of his and emerged with five rays. These rays are the sense organs (buddhīndriyas) by which he eats the objects of the senses. His organs of action (karmendriyas) are the horses, his chariot is the body, the mind is the driver, and primordial nature (prakṛti) is his whip.
Indeed, this body revolves when impelled, like a wheel; and once dead, this body is no longer established as possessing consciousness, for he is its impeller. || 2.9 ||

This very Self, as it were led by that [Pradhāna], as if overcome by the fruits of actions—both white and black—wanders through various bodies; because of its unmanifested nature, subtlety, invisibility, ungraspability, and lack of possessiveness, it is without fixed abode, and though non-doing, it stands as if it were the doer. 2.10.

Indeed, this [Self] is pure, firm, immovable, untainted, undistracted, free from longing, and stands like a spectator; it remains eating its own food, established with itself concealed behind a veil consisting of the qualities (guṇas)—thus it is "established. Thus ends the second chapter.

They said: "O Blessed One, if you thus indicate the majesty of this Self, then who is this other, supreme Self, who—overpowered by the fruits of white and black actions—attains good and evil wombs, and who, being overcome by pairs of opposites, wanders about in states that are downward or upward? To them he said: "Which one is this? [3.1]

Indeed, there is another, distinct elemental self (bhūtātman), which—overpowered by the fruits of white and black actions—attains good and evil wombs, wandering about, overcome by pairs of opposites, through upward or downward courses. This is its detailed explanation: the five subtle elements (tanmātras) are denoted by the word "elements" (bhūta), and the five gross elements (mahābhūtas) are also denoted by the word "elements. Now, that which is their aggregate is called the "body" (śarīra). And that which is indeed called the "body" is [the elemental self].

It has been said that the self is composed of the elements (bhūtātman). Yet, as it is said, "there exists for that [self] another self, like a drop upon a lotus leaf. Indeed, this [elemental self] is overwhelmed by the qualities of nature (prākṛta-guṇas); because of being thus overwhelmed, it falls into a state of delusion. Being deluded, it does not perceive the Lord, the Blessed One, who resides within itself as the Master and the Impeller. Satiated by the flood of qualities, it becomes turbid, unstable, fickle, greedy, distracted, and full of egoism. Thinking "I am that" and "this is mine," it binds itself by means of itself.
Like a bird caught in a net, being overcome by the fruits of what has been done, it wanders about. || 3.2 ||

Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere: "He who is the agent is indeed this *bhūtātman* (the elemental self); the inner person (*antar-puruṣa*) is the one who causes [action] to be performed by means of the instruments. Now, just as a lump of iron, overcome by fire, assumes various forms when struck by smiths, even so, indeed, this *bhūtātman*, overcome by the inner person and struck by the qualities (*guṇas*), assumes various forms. Furthermore, that which consists of the three qualities, which has evolved into eighty-four hundred thousand wombs, and which is the triple nature of the elements—this is the form of diversity. These very qualities are impelled by the person."

"As a wheel [follows] the potter," it is said; furthermore, just as when a mass of iron is being struck, the fire within it is not overcome, so too that Puruṣa is not overcome. This elemental self (bhūtātman), however, is overcome because of its close attachment [to the body]. || 3.3 ||

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "This body arises solely from sexual intercourse; it is devoid of consciousness, like a mere pit. As it emerges through the urinary passage, it is built up with bones, smeared with flesh, bound together with skin, and filled with feces, urine, bile, phlegm, marrow, fat, muscle-fat, and many other impurities—it lies there like a decaying chest. (3.4)

Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere: delusion, fear, despondency, sleep, drowsiness, wounds, old age, grief, hunger, thirst, meanness, anger, atheism, crookedness, envy, jealousy, lack of compassion, stupidity, shamelessness, deceitfulness, arrogance, and imbalance—these are associated with *tamas*. Thirst, affection, passion, greed, violence, attachment, preoccupation with views, envy, desire, instability, fickleness, the wish to take, the acquisition of wealth, and the favoring of friends—[these are associated with *rajas*].

Attachment to objects of the senses that are undesirable is aversion, while clinging to those that are desirable is passion. Overwhelmed by these qualities associated with *rajas*, this elemental self (*bhūtātman*) attains various forms; thus it is said, "it attains. (3.5) The Third Chapter.

Then those whose vital energies were drawn upward (the *ūrdhvaretas*), being greatly amazed, approached him closely and said: "Venerable sir, salutations to you! Teach us; you are our refuge, for no other is found. Who is this guest of the self (*bhūtātman*) by whom, having abandoned this [body], one attains union (*sāyujya*) with another? He said to them: 4.1.1.107–108. "The guest of the self is the breath (*prāṇa*). For when the breath departs from this body, it takes away all these vital functions (*prāṇa*) and unites them with its own nature. Therefore, the breath is the guest of the self. By means of that [breath], one attains union with another. 4.1.1.109–110. "But what is the nature of that other? Is it the earth, water, fire, air, or space? They replied: "No, sir. He said: "It is neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor air, nor space. It is the immortal Brahman, free from old age, death, fear, and sorrow. Having abandoned this body through the breath, one attains union with that [Brahman]. 4.1.1.111–112. "Now, how does one attain union? When the breath departs from this body, it carries away the voice, the eyes, the ears, the mind, and the sense of touch. Then, having abandoned this body, one attains union with that [Brahman]. 4.1.1.113–114. "Just as a leech (*jalaukā*), having moved from one blade of grass to another, abandons its former position, so the self, having moved from this body to another, abandons its former state. Thus, having abandoned this body, one attains union with that [Brahman]. 4.1.1.115–116. "Just as a caterpillar (*pipīlaka*), having reached the tip of a blade of grass, draws itself forward and makes a new connection, so the self, having moved from this body to another, abandons its former state. Thus, having abandoned this body, one attains union with that [Brahman]. 4.1.1.117–118. "Just as a goldsmith, having taken a piece of gold, fashions another form that is more beautiful than the previous one, so the self, having cast off this body and dispelled ignorance, creates for itself another, more beautiful form—whether it be that of the ancestors, the Gandharvas, the gods, or Prajāpati, or even that of Brahmā. Thus, having abandoned this body, one attains union with that [Brahman]. 4.1.1.119–120. "Therefore, knowing this, one should not grieve, nor be deluded. One should know: 'I am indeed that immortal Brahman, free from old age, death, fear, and sorrow. Having known this, one becomes a sage (*muni*). 4.1.1.121–122. "And he who knows this becomes a true knower of Brahman. He is not born again. He does not die. He is not shaken. He is not afflicted. He is the immortal Brahman. This is the truth.
