Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: His past deeds turn him back like waves upon great rivers; the arrival of death is as unavoidable as the tide of the ocean. Bound by the snares consisting of the fruits of good and evil, he is like a tethered animal. Like one held in captivity, he lacks independence; like one situated in the realm of Yama, he is in a state of manifold fear. He is intoxicated with the intoxication of pride like one drunk on wine; he is whirled about like one seized by a demon; he is afflicted by calamity like one bitten by a great serpent; and he is like one in a vast darkness.

Blinded by passion, it is like a magical illusion, composed of *māyā*, and like a dream—a false perception as insubstantial as the core of a plantain tree. Like an actor in a momentary costume, it is falsely beautiful, like a painted wall; thus it has been said. Those objects such as sound, touch, and the rest, though appearing as if they were not objects at all, persist in their nature. The individual soul (*bhūtātman*), however, being attached to them, does not remember the supreme state. (4.2)

Indeed, this is the remedy for the self that has become [worldly]: namely, the practice of the Dharma attained through knowledge, proceeding through one's own stages of life (āśramas). One's own duty (svadharma) alone sustains everything, just as the trunk supports the other branches; by this, one becomes oriented toward the higher realms, whereas otherwise one falls downward. He who does not become an ascetic (āśramin) by transgressing his own duty within the Vedas, but remains established in his own stages of life, is called an ascetic (tapasvin). This too has been said: there is no attainment of the realization of the Self for one who lacks austerity.

Or rather, it is the purification of karma; for thus it has been said: "By austerity, *sattva* is attained; from *sattva*, the mind is attained; by the mind, the Self is attained; and through the attainment of the Self, one ceases [from rebirth]. (4.3)

On this subject, there are these verses: Just as a fire without fuel is extinguished in its own source, so the mind, through the cessation of its fluctuations, is extinguished in its own source. (1) For one whose mind is extinguished in its own source and who moves toward truth, the objects of the senses—which follow the power of karma—are unreal for him, as he is no longer deluded by them. (2) The mind alone is indeed the cycle of existence; therefore, one should purify it with effort. Whatever the mind is, that one becomes; this is the eternal secret. (3)

For by the serenity of the mind, one destroys both auspicious and inauspicious karma; with a serene self, established in the Self, one enjoys imperishable happiness. (4) When the mind of a living being is attached to the realm of sense objects, if it were likewise directed toward Brahman, who would not be liberated from bondage? (5) The mind is said to be of two kinds: pure and indeed impure. The impure is characterized by desire and volition; the pure is devoid of desire. (6) Having made the mind perfectly steady, free from both dissolution and distraction—

When it reaches the state of non-mind, then that is the supreme state. (7) One should restrain [the mind] within the heart until it has reached dissolution; this alone is both knowledge and liberation, while all else are merely extensive elaborations of books. (8) The bliss that one obtains when the mind—its impurities shaken off by *samādhi* and established in the Self—is not possible to describe with words; at that time, it is grasped by the inner organ itself. (9) Just as water does not perceive water, nor fire in fire, nor space in space, one does not perceive [the Self].

In this way, the person is liberated when the mind has entered within. (10) The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings; it is held that when attached to sense objects it leads to bondage, and when free from sense objects it leads to liberation. (11) Now, here is this praise by Kautsāyani: "You are Brahmā, and you are indeed Viṣṇu; you are Rudra and you are Prajāpati. You are Agni, Varuṇa, and Vāyu; you are Indra and you are the Moon. (12)

You are Manu, you are Yama, you are the Earth, and you are the Imperishable (Acyuta). For the sake of your own purpose and for the sake of your innate nature, you abide manifoldly in heaven. O Lord of the Universe, salutations to you! You are the Soul of the Universe, the Creator of the Universe, the Enjoyer of the Universe, the Source of universal illusion, and the Lord whose delight is the play of the universe. Salutations to you, the peaceful Self; salutations to the most secret one; salutations to the inconceivable, the immeasurable, and the one without beginning or end.

This was indeed darkness alone in the beginning. Then, impelled by that which is beyond it, it attains the state of being an object; this is indeed the form of *rajas*. That *rajas*, when impelled, attains the state of inequality; this is indeed the form of *tamas*. That *tamas*, when impelled, flows forth from *tamas*; this is indeed the form of *sattva*. That *sattva*, when impelled, flows forth from *sattva*; this is that portion which is mere consciousness, the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) for each person, characterized by volition, determination, and self-conceit—this is Prajāpati. His...

The foremost bodies have been declared to be Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu. Now, that which is indeed his *rājasa* portion is this very Brahmā; that which is indeed his *tāmasa* portion is this very Rudra; and that which is indeed his *sāttvika* portion is this very Viṣṇu. He, being one, has become threefold, and has emerged as eightfold, elevenfold, twelvefold, and infinitefold. Because he has thus emerged, he moves among the beings as their foundation.
"He became the lord of all beings"—thus [it is said that] this Self is both within and without, and both within and without. The Fourth Chapter.

This one indeed sustains himself in two ways: that which is the vital breath (prāṇa) and that which is yonder Āditya. Now, these two were originally one, but they became fivefold by name: internally and externally, as day and night, they revolve. Yonder Āditya is the external self (bahirātman), and the vital breath is the internal self (antarātman). The external self is inferred by the movement of the internal self.

"Movement"—thus indeed it is said. Whatever wise man there may be who is free from evil, a presiding witness, pure-minded, established in that, with his gaze turned inward—he, having reached the inner self, infers the outer self as "movement. Thus indeed it is said: "Now, this golden person who is within the sun, who sees me as golden—he is this one who, residing within the lotus of the heart, eats the food. 5.1.

Now, he who dwells within the lotus of the heart and eats food—he is that very Agni, the solar fire dwelling in heaven, called Time, invisible, who eats the food of all beings. What is this lotus? Does one know it? This lotus is this space (ākāśa); its four quarters, the four intermediate directions, and their junctions are its petals. This Agni is on this side of it; beyond these two, Prāṇa and Āditya, are situated. One should worship these two with the syllable *om*, with the *vyāhṛtis*, and with the *Sāvitrī* verse. || 5.2 ||

There are indeed two forms of Brahman: the formed (mūrta) and the formless (amūrta). Now, that which is formed is the unreal; that which is formless is the real. That which is the real is Brahman; that which is Brahman is light; that which is light is the Āditya. This very one is the Self (Ātman) consisting of the syllable *om*. He divided himself threefold. The syllable *om* has three morae (*mātrā*). By these, all this is woven across and woven lengthwise within Him. For thus it is said: "One should meditate upon the Āditya as *om*, and thus yoke oneself to the Self. 5.3.

Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere: "Now, that which is the *udgītha* is the *praṇava*; that which is the *praṇava* is the *udgītha*. This sun is indeed the *udgītha*, the *praṇava*. For thus he said: "The *udgītha* is the leader named *praṇava*, free from name and form, sleepless, ageless, and deathless; again, it is fivefold, hidden in the cave of the heart. And thus he said: "With its root above and branches extending down to Brahmā, this entire world—consisting of ether, air, fire, water, earth, and so forth—is consumed by the One; this is Brahman, and this is yours."

Since this sun is that very syllable *om*, therefore one should worship it with this [syllable] *om* incessantly. Thus one should cause another to understand its essence. For thus it has been said: "This very syllable is meritorious; this very syllable is to be known. Whatever anyone desires after knowing this syllable, that he obtains. (5.4)

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "That which is 'Om' is his body that thunders; it possesses gender, as it is feminine, masculine, and neuter. It is radiant, as it is fire, wind, and the sun. It is sovereign, as it is Rudra and Viṣṇu. It possesses a mouth, as it is the Gārhapatya, Dakṣiṇāgni, and Āhavanīya fires. It knows, as it is the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman. It possesses the worlds, as it is Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ. It possesses time, as it is the past, the present, and the future. It is breath, fire, and the sun."

"This [syllable] is possessed of majesty, for it is food, water, and the moon; this is possessed of nourishment. This is possessed of consciousness, for it is intellect, mind, and ego; this is possessed of life-force, according to some, for it is prāṇa, apāna, and vyāna. When one says 'I renounce,' these [functions] are said to be surrendered to it. For thus it is said: 'O Satyakāma, this syllable "Om" is indeed both the higher and the lower. (5.5)

Now, this was indeed opened up; Prajāpati, having performed austerity, uttered it as *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. This, indeed, is the most substantial body of Prajāpati, the one possessing worlds. Of this [body], *svaḥ* is the head, *bhuvaḥ* the navel, and *bhūḥ* the feet. The sun is fixed as the eye of the Great Puruṣa; for by means of the eye, this [Puruṣa] moves through measures (*mātrā*). The eye is truth, for when established in the eyes, a person speaks regarding all matters. Therefore, one should worship *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, for it is food.

"Prajāpati, the self of all, becomes worshipped as if he were the eye of the universe. For thus it says: "This indeed is the body of Prajāpati that sustains the universe; in this, all this is contained, and this is contained within all this. Therefore, one should worship her. (5.6)

Regarding the verse "Tat savitur vareṇyam" (That excellent glory of Savitṛ): Savitṛ is indeed yonder sun; the knowers of Brahman say that he is thus to be chosen by one who desires the Self. Then, regarding "Bhargo devasya dhīmahi" (We meditate on the glory of the god): Savitṛ is indeed established in those [lights]; the knowers of Brahman say, "Which of his glories shall we contemplate? Then, regarding "Dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt" (Who may impel our thoughts): "Thoughts" (*dhiyaḥ*) are indeed the intellects; the knowers of Brahman say, "He who may impel these of ours. Then, regarding "Bharga": it is that which is placed within this sun, within the pupil of the eye.

This is called Bharga; for his movement is by means of lights, thus he is Bharga; indeed, he burns, thus he is Bharga—so say the exponents of Brahman. Furthermore, "Bharga" because he illuminates these worlds; "Bharga" because he delights these beings; "Gacchati" (he goes) because these creatures go toward him and come from him. Therefore, because he causes burning (*bhāraka*), he is Bharga; because he is pressed out (*sūyamāna*), he is Sūrya; because of impelling (*savana*), he is Savitṛ; because of giving (*dāna*), he is Āditya; because of purifying (*pavana*), he is Pāvamāna. Furthermore, "Āya" and "Āyanāt" (from coming); thus he is Āditya—for so it has been said.

Indeed, the Self—called the Immortal—is the knower, the thinker, the goer, the creator, the one who causes joy, the agent, the speaker, the taster, the smeller, and the toucher; it is the pervasive one established within the body. Thus it is said. But where consciousness has become dualistic, there indeed one hears, sees, smells, tastes, touches, and the Self knows all. Where, however, consciousness has become non-dualistic—freed from cause and effect, indefinable, incomparable, and beyond description—what, my dear, can be said of that?

For this indeed is the Self, the Lord, Śambhu, Bhava, Rudra, Prajāpati, the Creator of the Universe, Hiraṇyagarbha, Truth, Prāṇa, Haṃsa, the Peaceful, Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Arka, Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, Samrāj, Indra, Indu—He who shines there, veiled by fire, by the thousand-eyed golden one, by bliss. This indeed is what must be conquered, sought after; having granted freedom from fear to all beings, having gone to the forest, one perceives Him beyond one's own body, having cast out the objects of the senses. Thus [he perceives] Him.

The omniform, golden-hued, knower of all births, the ultimate refuge, the singular light that blazes—this Sun, the breath of all creatures, rises with a thousand rays, manifesting in a hundred ways. Thus ends the fifth chapter.

Now begins the sixth lesson. This one, who is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and that which is yonder sun (*āditya*)—these two indeed sustain themselves in a twofold manner. Furthermore, these two paths of his are internal and external; by means of day and night, these two revolve. Yonder sun is the external self (*bahirātman*), and the vital breath is the internal self (*antarātman*). Therefore, by the movement of the external self, the movement of the internal self is inferred. For thus it is said: "Now, whoever is wise, whose evil has been destroyed, who is the overseer of the senses, pure-minded, established therein, with eyes turned inward—he [perceives] by means of the movement of the internal self."

"The movement of the inner self is inferred from that which is outside"—thus it was said. Now, that golden person who is within the sun, who looks down upon this golden earth—he, indeed, is seated within the lotus of the heart and eats food. 6.1.6.1.

Now, he who dwells within the lotus of the heart and eats food—this is that very fire which, dwelling in the sky as the solar deity known as Time, is invisible and eats all beings as its food. What is this lotus, and of what is it composed? This very space is indeed that lotus; these four quarters and four intermediate directions are situated as its petals. These two—the vital breath (Prāṇa) and the sun—move back and forth within it. One should worship them with the syllable "Om," with the Vyāhṛtis, and with the Sāvitrī verse. || 6.2 ||

There are indeed two forms of Brahman: the formed and the formless. Now, that which is formed is unreal; that which is formless is real. That is Brahman; that is the light; that which is the light is the Āditya. This very one became the Self consisting of the syllable *om*. He divided himself threefold. "Om" consists of three morae (*mātrās*); by these, all this is woven across and woven lengthwise. Thus he said: "One should meditate upon the Āditya as 'Om' and thus yoke the Self. (6.3)

Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere: "Now, that which is the *udgītha* is the *praṇava*, and that which is the *praṇava* is the *udgītha*; indeed, yonder sun is the *udgītha*, and this [sun] is the *praṇava*."

For thus it is said: "The Udgītha, known as the Praṇava, the leader, whose form is light, free from sleep, free from old age, free from death, three-footed, consisting of three syllables, and further to be known as fivefold, is hidden in the cave of the heart. And thus it is said: "Brahman has its root above and three feet; the branches are space, air, fire, water, earth, and so forth. This one, named Aśvattha, is this Brahman. Its splendor is that which is the sun. And this belongs to the syllable 'Om'; therefore, one should worship this with 'Om' incessantly"—this is one [aspect] of it.
Thus he spoke to awaken [the listener]: "This very syllable is meritorious; this very syllable is supreme. Having known this very syllable, whatever one desires, that shall be his. (6.4)

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "This body of his is resonant with the sound 'Om'; it possesses gender as female, male, and neuter; it is radiant as fire, wind, and the sun; it possesses sovereignty as Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu; it possesses mouths as the Gārhapatya, Dakṣiṇāgni, and Āhavanīya fires; it possesses discernment as the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman; it possesses worlds as Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar; it possesses time as the past, present, and future; and it possesses life-breath as Agni and Sūrya."

"This [Om] is possessed of majesty, for it is food, water, and the moon; thus it is possessed of nourishment. It is possessed of consciousness, for it is intellect, mind, and ego; thus it is possessed of sentience. It is possessed of vital breath, for it is prāṇa, apāna, and vyāna; thus it is possessed of life-force. Therefore, when 'Om' is uttered, these [qualities] are introduced, honored, and established. For thus it has been said: 'O Satyakāma, this syllable "Om" is indeed both the higher and the lower Brahman. (6.5)

Now, this [universe] was indeed unuttered. That Prajāpati, who is Truth, having performed austerity, uttered it after: "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. This very [utterance] is the most substantial body of that Prajāpati, namely that which possesses the worlds. Of this [utterance], "svaḥ" is the head, "bhuvaḥ" is the navel, and "bhūḥ" is the feet; the sun is the eye. For the eye is the great measure of a person, since by means of the eye a person traverses the measures. The eye is indeed truth, for established in the eye, a person moves among all objects.

"Therefore, one should worship [the body] with the words 'bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. For by this, Prajāpati, the Self of All, comes to be worshipped as if he were the eye of the universe. Thus it is said: "This indeed is the all-sustaining body of Prajāpati; in this everything is contained, and in everything this is contained. Therefore, one should worship it. 6.6.

Regarding the verse, "Tat savitur vareṇyam" (That excellent glory of Savitṛ): the Brahman-knowers say that Savitṛ is indeed the Sun, and he is to be chosen by one who desires the Self. Then, regarding "Bhargo devasya dhīmahi" (We meditate on the glory of the God): the Brahman-knowers say that Savitṛ is indeed the God, and we meditate upon that which is called his "glory" (bhargas). Then, regarding "Dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt" (Who may impel our thoughts): the Brahman-knowers say that "thoughts" (dhīs) are indeed the intellects (buddhis), and [we pray] "who may impel those of us. Now, regarding "Bharga": it is that which is placed within yonder Sun, and that which is in the eye.

This is indeed Bharga; for his movement is by means of light (*bhābhiḥ*), thus he is Bharga; or because he burns (*bharjayati*), thus he is Bharga—so say the exponents of Brahman. Furthermore, *bha* because he illuminates these worlds; *ra* because he delights these beings; *ga* because these creatures go (*gacchanti*) into him and come (*āgacchanti*) from him. Therefore, because of his being the refuge (*bhara-gatvāt*), he is Bharga. Because he is eternally being born (*śāśvat sūyamānāt*), he is Sūrya. Because of his impelling (*savanāt*), he is Savitṛ. Because of his taking up (*ādānāt*), he is Āditya. Because of his purifying (*pavanāt*), he is Pāvana. And because of his nourishing (*āpyāyanāt*), he is Apaḥ. For thus it is said: "He is truly the Self of the Self."

"The pervasive Lord, when situated within the body, is the knower, the thinker, the perceiver, the goer, the one who has cast off [desires], the bestower of bliss, the agent, the speaker, the taster, the smeller, the seer, the hearer, and the toucher. Thus indeed it is said: "Now, where consciousness has become dualistic, there indeed one hears, sees, smells, tastes, touches, and the Self knows everything. But where consciousness has become non-dualistic—freed from cause, effect, and action, indefinable, incomparable, and beyond description—what can that be called?

For this indeed is the Self, the Lord, Śambhu, Bhava, Rudra, Prajāpati, the Creator of the universe, Hiraṇyagarbha, Truth, Prāṇa, Haṃsa, the Teacher, Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Arka, Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Samrāj, Indra, and Indu. He who shines there like fire enveloped by fire, within a golden egg with a thousand eyes—this very one is to be desired to be known, to be sought after; having granted fearlessness to all beings, having gone to the forest and cast out the objects of the senses from his own body, he should perceive Him.

"Regarding this one": the omniform, golden Jātavedas, the ultimate refuge, the sole light that blazes; with a thousand rays existing in a hundred ways, this Sun rises as the life-breath of all creatures. (6.8)

Therefore, one who knows this as having both natures meditates upon the Self alone and sacrifices to the Self alone. Thus meditation is praised by the wise as the mind established in the performance [of sacrifice]. One should purify that mind with the verse: "The mind defiled by impurity, the mind struck by leavings"—with this, one should purify it. He recites the mantra: "That which is defiled by leavings, that which is given by a sinner, or from a death-impurity or birth-impurity—may the purifier of Vasu, Agni, and the rays of Savitṛ purify my food and whatever other evil there may be. With water he first surrounds [the food] for the sake of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

He offers oblations with five [mantras]: "Svāhā to the out-breath! Svāhā to the diffused breath! Svāhā to the level-breath! Svāhā to the up-breath! Svāhā! Then, restraining his speech, he eats what remains; thereafter, he again covers [the food] from above with water. Having sipped water and become self-sacrificing, he should meditate upon himself with two [mantras]: "The breath is Agni; you are the All. And: "The breath is Agni, the Supreme Self; indeed, the fivefold wind has taken refuge in him. May he, being pleased, please the All—the consumer of all. You are the All; you are Vaiśvānara; by you the All is sustained."

"May all oblations enter you as you are being born; may all creatures be where you are, for you are the immortal of the universe"—by this very rite, one indeed returns again to the state of being the eater. 6.9.

Now, furthermore, another subsequent modification of this sacrifice to the Self (*ātmayajña*) should be understood, namely: "the food and the eater of food. Its detailed explanation is as follows: the conscious person (*puruṣa*), situated within *pradhāna*, is the enjoyer who consumes the food consisting of *prakṛti*. Of that [enjoyer], this elemental self (*bhūtātman*) is indeed the food, and its maker is *pradhāna*. Therefore, that which consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) is the object of enjoyment, and the person situated within is the enjoyer. In this regard, the proof is perception, because animals arise from seeds; therefore, by this very fact, the seed is the object of enjoyment for *pradhāna*.

The state of being food has been explained; therefore, the Puruṣa is the enjoyer and Prakṛti is the object of enjoyment. Abiding therein, he enjoys the "food" consisting of the constituents of Prakṛti—namely, the subtle body (*liṅga*) beginning with Mahat and ending with the specific elements (*viśeṣa*), which evolves through the distinctions of the three *guṇas*. By this very [explanation], the fourteenfold path has been explained. For this world, having become "food," is characterized by pleasure, pain, and delusion. Indeed, there is no grasping of sweetness by a seed until its production [as a sprout]; likewise, even for that [seed], it possesses the nature of food in its three stages, beginning with childhood.

Just as youth transforms into old age and that very [youth] becomes diminished, so too does the perception of the primary cause (pradhāna) occur once it has attained manifestation. In that state, the intellect and the other faculties become "delicious food" (anna), consisting of determination, volition, and self-consciousness. Then, the objects of the five senses likewise become delicious food; in this way, all the functions of the senses and the functions of the vital breaths are food. Thus, the manifest is food and the unmanifest is food. Its enjoyer is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa); because of its status as an enjoyer, its consciousness is well-established. Of that [enjoyer], fire is indeed the provider of food among the gods.

"Soma is food; by fire alone is food [consumed]. One who knows this—this elemental self known as Soma and also known as Agni, according to the statement "having the Unmanifest as its mouth"—is indeed a person who, through the mouth of the Unmanifest, experiences the three qualities (*guṇas*). He who knows thus is a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*), a yogi, and a self-sacrificer (*ātmayājī*). Furthermore, just as one does not touch women who have entered an empty house, so too he who does not touch the objects of the senses even when they have entered [the senses] is a renunciant, a yogi, and a self-sacrificer. (6.10)

Food, indeed, is the supreme form of the self, for this vital breath (*prāṇa*) consists of food. Now, if one does not eat, one becomes a non-thinker, a non-hearer, a non-toucher, a non-seer, a non-speaker, a non-smeller, and a non-taster, and one gives up the vital breaths. Thus it is said: "But if, indeed, one eats, having become enriched by the vital breaths, one becomes a thinker, a hearer, a toucher, a speaker, a taster, a smeller, and a seer. Thus it is said: "From food, indeed, creatures are born—those which..."
Some depend upon the earth; therefore they live by food alone, and in the end, they even pass away into this very [earth]. 6.11.

Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere: "Indeed, all these beings fall every day, desiring to seize food. The sun takes up that food with its rays; by means of that food, he shines. Anointed with food, these vital breaths (prāṇas) digest. Fire indeed blazes through food. This world was fashioned by Brahmā out of a desire for food. Therefore, one should meditate upon food as the Self. Thus it says: "From food beings are born; once born, they grow by food. It is eaten and it eats beings; therefore it is called 'food' (anna)."

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "This body which is food is indeed the form of the blessed Viṣṇu; breath is the essence of food, mind is the essence of breath, and consciousness is the essence of mind, while bliss is the essence of consciousness. He who knows this becomes possessed of food, possessed of breath, possessed of mind, possessed of consciousness, and possessed of bliss. As many beings as there are here that eat food, so much food does he eat, abiding within them, who knows this. Food alone is the conqueror of old age; food is remembered as the means of unification.
Food is the life-breath of animals; food is the eldest; food is remembered as the physician. || 6.13 ||

Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere: "Food is the source of all this, and time is the source of food; the sun is the source of time. Its form is that which is composed of the year consisting of twelve [months], beginning from the moments (nimeṣa) and so forth. Half of this is fiery (āgneya) and half is watery (vāruṇa). The half beginning with Maghā up to the middle of Śraviṣṭhā is fiery, proceeding in direct and reverse order; the half beginning with Āśleṣā up to the end of the middle of Śraviṣṭhā is lunar (saumya). Therein, each part of the self consists of nine divisions along with its movements; because of its subtlety, this measure is measured by this very means."

Indeed, there is no perception of the object of knowledge (prameya) without the means of knowledge (pramāṇa); yet the object of knowledge also attains the status of a means of knowledge for the sake of self-awakening through its distinctness. Thus it is said: "As many as are the parts of Time, so many [parts] does he move through who meditates upon Time as Brahman; Time recedes far away from him. And thus it is said: "From Time flow forth all beings, through Time they attain growth, and in Time they set; Time is both the formed and the formless. (6.14)

There are indeed two forms of Brahman: Time and Non-Time. Now, that which is prior to the sun is Non-Time; it is without parts. But that which begins with the sun is Time; it is with parts. This year is indeed the form of that which has parts. From the year, verily, these creatures are born; by the year, once born, they grow here; and in the year they pass away. Therefore, the year is Prajāpati, Time, Food, Brahman, the Nest, and the Self. Thus it is said: "Time ripens all beings."
All these indeed reside within the Great Self; he in whom time itself is cooked—he who knows that is a knower of the Veda. || 6.15 ||

This King of Rivers (the ocean) is Time personified; he is the one established therein who is called the Sun, from whom these—the moon, the stars, the planets, the years, and so forth—are produced. From them, whatever exists here, whether auspicious or inauspicious, is seen in this world. Therefore, because of these, the Sun is the Self of Brahmā; thus, one should worship the Sun under the name of Time. Some say, "The Sun is Brahmā. For it is said: "He is the priest, the enjoyer, the oblation, the mantra, the sacrifice, Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, the All, the Something, the Lord, and the Witness—he who shines in that orb. || 6.16 ||

In the beginning, indeed, this was Brahman alone—endless in the east, endless in the south, endless in the west, endless in the north, endless above and below, and endless in every direction. For in its case, directions such as east and so forth are not applicable; nor are there horizontal, vertical, or upward dimensions. This Supreme Self is ungraspable, immeasurable, inconceivable, and of the nature of space. He alone, the one who is the destruction of all, remains awake. From this space, he indeed awakens this mere consciousness, and by him alone is this world meditated upon.

And when this [body] perishes, that radiant form of his vanishes—namely, that light which shines in yonder sun, in the smokeless fire, or that most wonderful light within the belly which digests food. For thus it is said: "That which is in the fire, that which is in the heart, and that which is in the sun—that is one and the same. Indeed, he who knows this attains oneness with the One. 6.17.

Likewise, the ritual procedure for that [practice] consists of the six limbs known as breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), meditation (dhyāna), concentration (dhāraṇā), reasoning (tarka), and absorption (samādhi); this is called Yoga. When, by means of this, the seer beholds the golden-hued Maker, the Lord, the Puruṣa who is the source of Brahman, then the wise one, having abandoned merit and sin, unifies everything in the supreme, imperishable state. For thus it is said: "Just as deer and birds do not resort to a mountain set ablaze, so too faults never take refuge in the knower of Brahman. (6.18)

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "When indeed the wise man, having restrained the mind externally and having caused the senses to enter within, should remain there free from conceptualization; for since the living being known as *prāṇa* has arisen here from that which is beyond *prāṇa*, therefore one should indeed hold the *prāṇa* in that which is called the Fourth (*turya*)—for thus it is said: 'The thoughtless thought situated in the midst of thought, inconceivable, secret, and supreme; therein the mind should be placed, and that sign is without support. (6.19)

Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere: "Beyond this is his supreme concentration (*dhāraṇā*), which consists of pressing the palate with the tip of the tongue, and the restraint of speech, mind, and breath. One perceives Brahman through inquiry when one sees the Self by means of the self—smaller than the smallest, radiant—as the mind is extinguished. Having seen the Self by means of the self, one becomes selfless; being selfless, he is the innumerable, the unborn, the inconceivable, characterized by liberation. This is the supreme secret. Thus it is said: "By the serenity of the mind, one destroys both auspicious and inauspicious karma.
With a serene self, established in the Self, one attains imperishable bliss. (6.20)

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "The upward-moving channel called Suṣumṇā is the path for the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa), severed within the palate. By means of that [channel], joined with the vital breath, the syllable Om (Oṃkāra), and the mind, one should ascend upwards. Having turned the tip [of the tongue] back against the palate and not engaging the sense organs, the Great One (mahimā) should behold the Greatness (mahiman). Thereafter, he goes beyond the state of having a self (nirātman); because of being without a self, he does not partake in pleasure or pain, and he attains isolation (kevalatva). Thus indeed says the Supreme: "Having first established [the body] and restrained the breath, then, having crossed to the further shore by the shoreless [path], one should subsequently join [the mind] to the summit. (6.21)

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "There are indeed two Brahmans to be meditated upon: the Word (*śabda*) and the Non-word (*aśabda*). Now, by means of the Word itself, the Non-word is revealed. Then, therein, the word 'Om'—having ascended upward by means of this—reaches its dissolution in the Non-word. This, they say, is the goal, this is the immortal, this is union with That (*tatsāyujyatva*), and this is liberation (*nirvṛtatva*). And just as a spider, having ascended upward by means of its thread, finds space, even so indeed does that meditator, having ascended upward by means of the syllable 'Om', attain independence.

Otherwise, others who are proponents of sound perceive the sound of the space within the heart through the practice of joining the ear with the thumb. This [sound] is of seven kinds; its analogies are as follows: a river, a small bell, bronze, a wheel, a frog, a bird, and a cricket, or as one says, "it speaks in a windless place. Having transcended that which has distinct characteristics, others have set [their minds] upon the wordless, unmanifest Brahman. There, they possess non-distinct attributes and are indistinguishable from one another, just as various juices, once combined, become honey. Thus it is said: "There are two Brahmans..."
One should know that there are two kinds of Brahman: the Brahman of Sound and the Supreme. One who is proficient in the Brahman of Sound attains the Supreme Brahman. (6.22)

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "That which is sound is this syllable *oṃ*. That which is its tip is the peaceful, soundless, fearless, sorrowless, blissful, satisfied, steady, immovable, immortal, infallible, and eternal, known by the name Viṣṇu; for the sake of attaining the state beyond all else, one should worship that. Thus it is said: 'He who is the supreme and inferior God named by the name Oṃ—soundless and become like the void—one should practice [meditation] upon him in the place of the head. (6.23)

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "The body is the bow, and 'Om' is the arrow; its point is the mind. Having pierced through the darkness characterized by ignorance, one reaches that which is beyond darkness. Then, having pierced through that [darkness], one beholds Brahman—which is radiant like the sun, full of splendor, flashing like a whirling firebrand, and situated beyond the darkness—that which shines in yonder sun, in the moon, in the fire, and in lightning. Indeed, having seen this, one attains immortality. Thus it is said: "Meditation is fixed within upon the supreme reality and upon the objects of focus."

Therefore, non-specific consciousness attains the specific. When the mental faculty has dissolved, that bliss which is witnessed by the Self—that is Brahman, the immortal, the pure; that is the goal, and that indeed is the world. || 6.24 ||

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "He who, with his senses withdrawn in sleep, beholds as if in a dream through a mind of supreme purity—uncontrolled within the cavity of the senses—the Leader named *praṇava*, whose form is light, free from sleep, free from old age, free from death, and free from sorrow—he too becomes named *praṇava*, the Leader, whose form is light, free from sleep, free from old age, free from death, and free from sorrow. For thus it has been said: "In this way, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the syllable *oṃ* [are one], because everything is manifoldly [derived] from them."

Because one joins (*yunakti*) or is joined (*yuñjate*) [to the Self], it is traditionally known as *yoga*. The unification of the vital breath, the mind, and likewise the senses, as well as the renunciation of all states of being, is designated as *yoga*. (6.25)

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "Just as a fowler, having caught water-birds with a stringed trap, offers them into the fire in his belly, even so, indeed, does he offer these vital breaths (*prāṇas*) into the fire of the body by means of this syllable 'Om'. Therefore, when heated, [the fire] blazes up; and just as clarified butter does not blaze up upon contact with grass or wood when merely heated, even so, indeed, does this [fire] called 'apāna' blaze up through contact with the 'prāṇa'. Now, that which blazes up is the form of Brahman, and this is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu."

This indeed is the Rudra-nature of Rudra; having divided himself into immeasurable parts, he fills these worlds. Thus it is said: "Just as sparks from a fire, and likewise rays from the sun, so too do the vital breaths (prāṇas) and the rest emerge from him here in their respective order. || 6.26 ||

Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "This heat of the body belongs to Brahman—the supreme, immortal, bodiless one; this [heat] is its clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Now, being manifest, it is deposited in the sky. Thus, with one-pointedness, they pierce the space within the heart, so that what is there becomes like light. Therefore, one quickly attains that state, just as an iron mass placed on the ground quickly attains the nature of the earth; or as smiths and others do not overcome an iron mass when it is in the form of clay.

"The mind perishes together with its support in this very manner; for thus it has been said: 'The sheath consisting of space within the heart is bliss, the supreme abode; from that comes our own yoga, as well as the radiance of fire and the sun. || 6.27 ||
Furthermore, it is said elsewhere:

"Having transcended the elements, the senses, and their objects, one should take up the bow whose string is fortitude and whose staff is self-control; and with an arrow consisting of non-conceit, having struck down that first gatekeeper of Brahman—whose crown is delusion, who wears thirst and envy as earrings, whose bowstring is sloth, whose staff is greed, and who has pride as his supervisor—one slays these very beings with an arrow consisting of desire. Having slain him, and having crossed to the further shore of the space within the heart by means of the boat of the syllable *Oṃ*, the intermediate space (*antarākāśa*) becomes manifest."

Just as one desiring to dig a pit slowly enters the pit itself, so too should one enter the hall of Brahman (*brahmaśālā*); then, by means of the Guru’s instruction, one should push open the four-gated treasury of Brahman (*brahmakośa*).

Thus, being pure, purified, void, tranquil, breathless, selfless, infinite, imperishable, stable, eternal, unborn, and independent, he abides in his own majesty. Having seen him thus abiding in his own majesty, one perceives the wheel of movement as if it were a wheel that has ceased to turn. For thus it is said regarding the embodied soul who is disciplined and eternally liberated after six months:
The infinite, supreme secret, the perfect yoga, proceeds.
For the embodied soul who is pierced by rajas and tamas, who is intensely inflamed by passion,
and who is attached to children, wife, and family, [this state] never occurs.

Having spoken thus, Śākāyanya vanished within his heart. Having paid homage to him, [the king reflected]: "O King, by means of this knowledge of Brahman, the sons of Prajāpati have ascended the path of Brahman. Through the practice of yoga, one attains contentment, endurance of the pairs of opposites, and tranquility. This most secret [teaching] should not be proclaimed to one who is not a son, nor to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who is not tranquil; it should be given only to one who is devoted to no other and endowed with all virtues. 6.29.

"Oṃ! In a pure place, being pure himself, established in goodness (*sattva*), studying the truth, speaking the truth, meditating on the truth, and performing sacrifice to the truth—one should become such. Therefore, one who has attained cessation through the true Brahman, which is characterized by the desire for truth, whose bonds are severed by the fruit of that state, and who is free from expectations, remains fearless toward others as if toward oneself; being desireless, he abides having ascended to imperishable and immeasurable bliss. Indeed, freedom from desire is the supreme extraction of the highest treasure, like that of a hoard.

For that person, consisting of all desires and characterized by determination, volition, and egoism, is bound; therefore, one who is the opposite of that is liberated. Regarding this, some say that the *guṇa* (quality), having attained the bondage of the self through determination by virtue of the differentiation of *prakṛti*, [is bound].

Liberation results from the destruction of defects through the cessation of mental determination (*adhyavasāya*). For it is by the mind alone that one sees, and by the mind that one hears. Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear—all these are indeed the mind. Carried away by the flood of the qualities (*guṇa*), defiled, unstable, wavering, being swept away, full of longing, and distracted, it arrives at a state of self-conceit. Thinking "I am that" and "this is mine," it thus binds itself by itself, like a bird caught in its own web.

Therefore, the person is bound by the marks of determination (*adhyavasāya*), volition (*saṅkalpa*), and egoism (*abhimāna*); consequently, one who is the opposite of that is liberated. For this reason, one should remain free from determination, free from volition, and free from egoism—this is the characteristic of liberation. This is the path to Brahman here; this is the opening of the door here, through which one will go beyond this darkness. For all desires are contained herein; regarding this, they cite the following: "When the five [sensory] cognitions, together with the mind, come to rest..."

"When the intellect no longer functions, they call that the supreme goal. Having said this, Śākāyanya vanished within his heart; having paid homage to him and performed the proper rites, he departed satisfied, like the wind toward the northern course—for there is no movement by a contrary path here. Regarding this, they cite the "Path of Brahman": "Having pierced the solar door, they emerge upward. It is said: "Infinite are his rays, which reside in the heart like a lamp—white, black, tawny, blue, tawny-brown, and soft red."

One ray of these stands above; having pierced the solar disc and transcended the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*), by it they go to the supreme goal. Another hundred rays of his that are situated upward by which he reaches the abodes of the hosts of gods. Those many rays of his below which are of gentle luster—for the enjoyment of karma in this world—he transmigrates by them, being subject to bondage. Therefore, this blessed Āditya is the cause of creation, heaven, and liberation. 6.30.

"What is the nature of these senses as they function, and who here is their originator and controller? To this he replies: "They have the Self (Ātman) as their nature. For the Self is indeed their originator. Furthermore, there are the Apsarases and the solar rays named Marīcis; with five of these rays, it consumes the objects of the senses. "Who is the Self? It is that which has been described by characteristics such as being pure, stainless, empty, and tranquil, and which is to be grasped by its own signs. This is the sign of that signless one: just as heat is the manifest sign of fire, so too is the most auspicious essence of water.

Thus say some. Then others say: speech, hearing, sight, mind, and breath; or others say: intellect, fortitude, memory, and wisdom—that is it. Now, these [proceed] from this very one, just as here [on earth] sprouts from a seed, or as smoke, flame, and sparks from fire. Regarding this they cite: "Just as sparks indeed from a fire, and rays from the sun, even so from him the vital breaths and the rest emerge again here in their respective order. (6.31)

From this very Self, indeed, all vital breaths, all worlds, all Vedas, all deities, and all beings emerge. Its secret name (*upaniṣad*) is "The Truth of Truth. Now, just as when wood that is wet is placed upon a fire, various clouds of smoke issue forth, even so from this Great Being, this is the breath: the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvāṅgirasa, history, ancient lore, sciences, secret doctrines (*upaniṣads*), verses, aphorisms, explanations, and commentaries—all these are but its breath;
all these beings are its own.

This Agni is the year, consisting of five bricks; its bricks are these: spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, and winter. This Agni, possessing a head, two wings, a back, a belly, and a tail, is the knower of man. This was the first layer of Prajāpati. Having lifted the sacrificer up to the intermediate space with his hands, he delivered him to Vāyu. Vāyu is indeed breath; Agni is breath. Its bricks are these: inhalation (*prāṇa*), exhalation (*vyāna*), downward breath (*apāna*), pervasive breath (*samāna*), and upward breath (*udāna*). This Agni possesses a head, two wings, a back, a belly, and a tail.

This intermediate space, which knows the Person, is the second layer of Prajāpati. With his hands, he lifted the sacrificer up to heaven and presented him to Indra. That sun up there is indeed Indra; he is this very Agni. His bricks are the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, Atharvāṅgirasa, Itihāsa, and Purāṇa. This Agni, who knows the Person, possesses a head, two wings, a tail, and a back. This sky is the third layer of Prajāpati. With his hands, he makes an offering for the sacrificer to the Knower of the Self (Ātmavit). Just as the Knower of the Self, having lifted [the self] up, presents it to Brahman, so does he become blissful and joyful therein. || 6.33 ||

The earth is the Gārhapatya fire, the intermediate space is the Dakṣiṇāgni, and the sky is the Āhavanīya. From these very [fires] arise Pavamāna, Pāvaka, and Śuci; by this, his sacrifice is made manifest. Since the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*) is indeed a combination of Pavamāna, Pāvaka, and Śuci, therefore Agni is to be sacrificed to, to be kindled, to be praised, and to be meditated upon. Having taken the oblation, the sacrificer desires meditation upon the deity: "The golden-colored bird, established in the heart and in the sun, the *madgu* and the swan, the bull of splendor—he, we worship in this fire."

And he also investigates the meaning of the mantra: "That excellent splendor of Savitṛ, which is to be meditated upon—[that splendor] which, abiding within the intellect, the meditator here follows as the state of peace of the mind and places it within the Self alone. On this point, there are these verses: 1. Just as a fire without fuel is extinguished in its own source, so the mind, through the cessation of its mental modifications (*vṛtti*), is extinguished in its own source. 2. For the mind that has been extinguished in its own source and whose desires have become true, the objects of the senses—which were previously delusive and followed the power of karma—become unreal.

3. The mind alone is indeed saṃsāra; one should purify it with effort. Whatever the mind is, that one becomes; this is an eternal secret. 4. For by the serenity of the mind, one destroys both auspicious and inauspicious karma. With a serene self, abiding in the Self, one enjoys imperishable bliss. 5. Just as the mind of a living being is intensely attached to the sphere of sense objects, if it were likewise [attached] to Brahman, who would not be liberated from bondage?

6. The mind is said to be of two kinds: pure and indeed impure. It is impure through contact with desire; it is pure when devoid of desire. 7. Having made the mind perfectly steady, free from both dissolution and distraction, when it reaches the state of non-mind, then that is the supreme state. 8. The mind should be restrained within the heart until it has reached its dissolution; this is both knowledge and liberation, while all others are merely extensive elaborations of books.

9. The bliss that arises when the mind, cleansed of impurities by *samādhi*, is established in the Self, cannot be described by speech; at that time, it is perceived by the inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) itself. 10. Just as water does not perceive water, nor fire in fire, nor space in space, so he whose mind has entered within is completely liberated. 11. The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings; attached to sense objects, it leads to bondage; free from sense objects, it is known as liberation.

Therefore, for those who have not performed the Agnihotra, who have not built the sacrificial fire-altar, and who do not contemplate with knowledge, the recollection of the void that is the state of Brahman is contrary [to their capacity]. Consequently, the fire must be worshipped, built, praised, and contemplated. 6.34.

Homage to Agni, who dwells on earth and remembers the world; grant a world to this sacrificer. Homage to Vāyu, who dwells in the intermediate space and remembers the world; grant a world to this sacrificer. Homage to Āditya, who dwells in heaven and remembers the world; grant a world to this sacrificer. Homage to Brahmā, who dwells in all and remembers all; grant everything to this sacrificer. The face of Truth is covered by a golden vessel. O Pūṣan, uncover it for Viṣṇu, whose nature is Truth, for him who is that [Brahman].

The person within the sun—He is indeed I. This is the true Dharma (Satyadharma), which is the solar nature of the sun. That white, signless person is merely a portion of the light situated within the sky; this is what is in the center of the sun, as it were. This is in the eye and in the fire. This is Brahman, this is the Immortal, this is Bharga. This is Satyadharma, merely a portion of the light situated within the sky; this is the nectar in the center of the sun, of which Soma is the essence, and the vital breaths (prāṇas) are the sprouts.

This is Brahman; this is the immortal; this is Bharga. This is the true Dharma, a mere fraction of the splendor situated within the firmament—namely, that Yajus which shines in the midst of the sun: *Om āpo jyotī raso 'mṛtaṃ brahma bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ om*.

The pure swan with eight feet, the thread of three strands, the subtle and imperishable; he who sees the two-fold dharma kindled by splendor sees everything. That which is in the midst of the sun, having risen, becomes two rays—this is the Savitṛ, this is true dharma, this is the Yajus, this is austerity, this is fire, this is wind, this is breath, this is water, this is the moon, this is the bright, this is the immortal, this is the sphere of Brahman, this is the light-ocean; in that very ocean is the sacrificer, like a lump of salt.

They seem to dissolve as it were; this indeed is the oneness of Brahman, for here all desires are contained. Regarding this, they cite: "Like a stream of liquid stirred by a subtle breeze, that which dwells within the gods flashes forth. He who knows thus is a knower of the Sun, a knower of duality, and one whose light is unified; he becomes of that very nature. Those [rays] which rise incessantly like drops, or like lightning from the glow of clouds in the highest heaven—those rays, by virtue of their support, appear like the matted locks of Fire (Kṛṣṇavartman) through his glory. (6.35)

Indeed, there are two forms of this Brahman-light: one is tranquil and the other is prosperous. Now, that which is tranquil has space as its support; and that which is prosperous has this [world] as its food. Therefore, one should sacrifice within the sacrificial altar with mantras, herbs, clarified butter, meat, sacrificial cakes, cooked offerings in pots, and so forth.

Considering that the remnants of food and drink remaining in the mouth are the *āhavanīya* fire, one should offer the *agnihotra* for the sake of the perfection of splendor, for the conquest of the worlds of merit, and for the attainment of immortality. Regarding this, they cite: "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra*; one attains the kingdom of Yama by means of the *agniṣṭoma*, the kingdom of Soma by the *uktha*, the kingdom of the Sun by the *ṣoḍaśin*, sovereign rule by the *atirātra*, and the realm of Prajāpati by a sacrifice lasting up to a thousand years. Just as a lamp remains steady through the union of the wick, the vessel, and the oil, so too do these two—the self and the pure [mind]—remain established through their internal application to the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*). (6.36)

Therefore, one should worship this immeasurable splendor with the syllable *Om*. It is declared to be threefold: in fire, in the sun, and in the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Now, this channel called "abundance of food" carries what is offered into the fire toward the sun. From that, the essence which flowed down rains as the *udgītha*. By that, these vital breaths exist, and from the vital breaths, living beings arise. Regarding this, they cite an example: "The oblation that is poured into the fire is made to go to the sun; the sun rains by means of its rays; through that, food comes into being; from food, the origin of all beings occurs. For thus it has been said.
An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun; from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings. || 6.37 ||

One who offers the *agnihotra* oblation pierces the net of greed; then, having cut through delusion and not being tormented by anger, while contemplating desire, he pierces the four-layered sheath of Brahman. Thence, having pierced the spheres of the sun, the moon, fire, and the *sāttvika*, he becomes pure. Therein lies the supreme space—the immovable, immortal, infallible, and eternal one known as Viṣṇu, the ultimate abode of all, endowed with the fulfillment of all desires and omniscience, the independent consciousness.

One sees him abiding in his own glory; regarding this they cite: "The moon is situated in the midst of the sun; in the midst of the moon is fire; in the midst of light is the *sattva*; and in the midst of the *sattva* stands the Imperishable (*acyuta*). Having meditated upon him who is the size of a thumb or a span within the body, yet subtler than the subtlest, one thereafter attains the supreme state; for all desires are contained therein. Regarding this they cite: "He who is the size of a thumb or a span within the body is indeed twofold or threefold, like the heat and the flame of a lamp."
That Brahman, being praised, the Great God entered the worlds. Om! Salutations to Brahman; salutations. Thus ends the sixth chapter.

7th Prapāṭhaka, Section 7. Agni, the Gāyatra, the Trivṛt-stoma, the Rathantara-sāman, the spring season, the vital breath (prāṇa), and the stars—the Vasus rise in the east, they heat, they rain, they praise, and they enter again. They look through the internal aperture; he is inconceivable, formless, profound, the enjoyer of qualities, free from illusion, the Lord of Yogins, omniscient, like a cloud, immeasurable, without beginning or end, glorious, unborn, wise, indefinable, the creator of all, the Self of all, the consumer of all, the ruler of all, and the innermost within all. 7.1.

Indra, the Triṣṭubh meter, the Pañcadaśa-stoma, the Bṛhat-sāman, the summer season, the Vyāna-vital breath, Soma, and the Rudras rise from the south; they heat, they rain, they praise, and they enter again. They look through the internal aperture. He is without beginning or end, unlimited, undivided, not to be employed by another, independent, signless, formless, possessed of infinite power—the Creator, the Maker of Light. 7.2.

The Maruts, the Jagatī meter, the seventeenfold Stoma, the Vairūpa Sāman, the rainy season, the downward breath, and the Śukra cup—the Ādityas rise from behind, they heat, they rain, they praise, and they enter again. Through the internal aperture, they behold that which is peaceful, soundless, fearless, sorrowless, blissful, satisfied, stable, immovable, immortal, infallible, constant, known as Viṣṇu, the ultimate abode of all. 7.3.

The Viśvedevas are the Anuṣṭubh meter, the twenty-one-fold chant, the Vairāja melody, and the autumn season; Varuṇa and the Sādhyas rise up from the north, they heat, they rain, they praise, and they enter again. Within the opening, they look; within, he is pure, cleansed, void, peaceful, breathless, selfless, and infinite. 7.4.

Mitra and Varuṇa; the Paṅkti, Triṇava, and Trayastriṃśa meters; the Śākvara and Raivata chants; the winter and the cool season; the upward vital breath (udāna); and the Aṅgirasas—these are the moon and the rays that rise upward, heat, rain, praise, and again enter. Through the internal aperture, they behold the leader named Praṇava, whose form is light, who is free from sleep, free from old age, free from death, and free from sorrow. 7.5.

Saturn, Rāhu, Ketu, serpents, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, men, birds, Śarabhas, elephants, and others rise up from below, heat, rain, praise, and then enter again; he who perceives through the internal aperture is the wise one—the sustainer, the innermost of all, the imperishable, the pure, the purified, the radiant, the patient, the peaceful. 7.6.

For this very Self within the heart is subtler than the tip of a hair, like a fire that has been extinguished, yet it is omniform. All this is its food; upon it these creatures are woven. This Self is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger and thirst, whose resolve is true, and whose desires are true. He is the Supreme Lord, He is the Sovereign of beings, He is the Protector of beings, He is the Bridge, the Sustainer. For this very Self is the Ruler, Śambhu, Bhava, Rudra, Prajāpati, the Creator of the universe, Hiraṇyagarbha, Truth, and Prāṇa.

The Haṃsa, the Praśasta, Acyuta, Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa—he who is in the fire, he who is here in the heart, and he who is yonder in the sun, he is this one. To him, the one of universal form, established in the true ether, salutation! 7.7.

Now, O King, these are the obstacles to knowledge; indeed, this is the source of the snare of delusion: that people cling to what is beneath them even when the gateway to heaven has been described before them by those who do not themselves go to heaven. Furthermore, there are others who are constantly delighted, constantly wandering, constantly begging, and constantly living by their crafts; and others who are city-beggars, beggars for whom sacrifices should not be performed, disciples of Śūdras, and Śūdras who are learned in the scriptures; and others who are flatterers, matted-hair ascetics, actors, soldiers, renunciants, and performers on the stage.

Those who engage in royal service, those who have fallen [from their vows], and others who, having set aside the welfare of the hosts of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Piśācas, Uragas, Grahas, and so forth, say, "We shall pacify them"—and furthermore, those others who are hypocritical Kaṣāyakuṇḍalins and Kāpālikas, and others who, through false logic, fallacies, trickery, and sorcery, seek to establish themselves among the followers of the Veda; one should not dwell with them, for they are indeed thieves who are exposed and lead away from heaven. Thus it is said: "Those who, having set aside the welfare of the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Piśācas, Uragas, Grahas, and so forth, say, 'We shall pacify them,' and those others who are hypocritical Kaṣāyakuṇḍalins and Kāpālikas, and others who, through false logic, fallacies, trickery, and sorcery, seek to establish themselves among the followers of the Veda—one should not dwell with them, for they are indeed thieves who are exposed and lead away from heaven. Thus it is said.
Deceived by the deceptions of those who preach selflessness, through false examples and reasons, the world wanders about and does not recognize that which lies beyond Vedic knowledge. || 7.8 ||

Bṛhaspati, having become Śukra, created this ignorance for the sake of Indra’s safety from the Asuras and for their destruction. By means of it, people designate the auspicious as inauspicious and the inauspicious as auspicious; they say, "Let there be meditation on the dharma that destroys the Vedas and other scriptures. Therefore, one should not speak of this [ignorance], for otherwise it is like a barren woman; its fruit is mere pleasure, like that of one who has fallen from his conduct. Thus it is said: "Far apart and divergent are these two: ignorance and what is known as knowledge."

I consider Naciketas to be desirous of knowledge; many desires do not entice you. He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together—having crossed over death by means of ignorance, he enjoys immortality by means of knowledge. Enveloped within ignorance, yet considering themselves wise and learned, the deluded wander about, stumbling like blind men led by one who is himself blind. (7.9)

The gods and the asuras, desiring to know the Self, went into the presence of Brahmā. Having paid homage to him, they said, "O Blessed One, we desire to know the Self; please teach it to us. Thereupon, having meditated for a long time, he reflected: "Those asuras are indeed of a different nature; what has been told to them is something other than this [true Self]. These fools subsist upon that, being full of attachment, striking down their enemies, and proclaiming falsehoods; they perceive the unreal as if it were real, like a magician’s trick. Therefore, that which is declared in the Vedas is the truth—indeed, that which is spoken in the Vedas is the truth.
The wise live depending upon that; therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not study what is non-Vedic, thinking, "May this be my purpose. 7.10.

This indeed is the true nature of that sky which is contained within the void: it is the supreme light, declared to be threefold—within fire, within the sun, and within the vital breath (prāṇa). This indeed is the true nature of that sky which is contained within the void: it is this syllable "Om. By means of this alone, one awakens, rises, and breathes; it is the eternal support for the intellect of Brahman. Indeed, having ascended by means of the branches from trunk to trunk, it moves within this very wind in the sky.

Regarding this, they cite examples such as the dissolution of salt in water, the cooling of the heat of clarified butter, or the expansion of one who meditates intensely. Now, why is it called "Vaidyuta" (the lightning-like)? Because as soon as it is uttered, it illuminates the entire body; therefore, one should worship this with the syllable "Om" as immeasurable splendor.
This person who resides in the right eye is Indra;
his wife resides in the left eye.
The union of those two occurs within the subtle essence inside the heart; that light of theirs is here indeed a single mass of both.
From the heart it comes forth and becomes established in this eye;
that channel (nāḍī) is the conduit for those two, being one yet divided into two.
The mind strikes the fire of the body; it impels the vital air (māruta).
Moving within the chest, that vital air produces the deep, resonant tone.
Know that through the union with the fire of the *khaja* [breath], a subtle atom (*aṇu*) joined in the heart becomes twice as subtle;
at the region of the throat it becomes a triad of atoms (*tryaṇuka*); and at the tip of the tongue, they say the *mātṛka* [syllable] has thus emerged.
One who does not see death does not see disease, nor even suffering;
for seeing everything, one sees all and attains everything in every way.
The visual, the dream-walker, the sleeping, and that which is beyond sleep—
these are its four divisions, and the fourth is greater than them.
One foot of Brahman moves within the three [lower worlds], and three feet move in the highest;
these serve for the experience of truth and falsehood, for the state of duality belongs to the Great Soul—yes, the state of duality belongs to the Great Soul. (7.11)
Thus ends the seventh chapter.
Oṃ, may they swell; thus [ends] the peace invocation.
Thus ends the Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad.
